Claude Sonnet 5.5 1.00M $2.00 $10.00 $0.100 95.0%
Gemini 4 Carbon 1.05M $2.00 $10.00 $0.100 95.0%
GPT-6.1 Terra Pro 1.05M $1.00 $5.00 $0.050 95.0%
Mistral Large 4 1.05M $0.70 $2.10 $0.070 90.0%
DeepSeek V4 Pro (0813) 1.05M $0.111 $4.44 $0.097 12.6%
Qwen 3.8 Flash 1.00M $0.15 $0.47 $0.016 89.3%
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1.05M $0.022 $0.40 $0.004 81.8%

Look closely at the Prefix Cache Read column:

  • GPT-6.1 Terra Pro ($0.05/1M cached read) is cheaper on cached long-context reads than Mistral Large 4 ($0.07/1M) and DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 ($0.097/1M), even though Terra Pro's uncached input price ($1.00/1M) is higher.
  • Conversely, if your prompt architecture accidentally busts the prefix cache, Terra Pro immediately jumps 20x on input ($0.05 -> $1.00/1M), and Claude Sonnet 5.5 jumps 20x ($0.10 -> $2.00/1M).

2. The 5-Minute vs. 1-Hour Cache TTL Break-Even

Most teams model prompt caching assuming every turn after Turn 1 gets the cached read rate. That works for autonomous coding or RAG loops where turns fire every 3-15 seconds and continuously refresh a 5-minute TTL.

Human-in-the-loop SaaS workflows behave differently:

  • A user asks an analyst copilot to summarize a 60K-token contract, reads the output for 7 minutes, and asks a follow-up question.
  • Under a 5-minute default TTL (1.25x write multiplier), the KV blocks have already been evicted. Every message pays full uncached input—or worse, repeatedly pays 1.25x cache-write fees that never get read!

If a provider offers an extended 1-hour TTL (2.0x write multiplier vs. 0.05x-0.10x read multiplier), when does paying 2.0x upfront beat paying uncached 1.0x per turn?

Static prefix = P tokens | Read multiplier r = 0.10x | Turns = N (>5 min apart)

Extended 1h Cache Cost = P * (2.0 + (N - 1) * 0.10)
Uncached Input Cost    = P * N

Break-even:
  2.0 + 0.10*N - 0.10 < N
  1.90 < 0.90*N
  N > 2.11 turns  -->  Breaks even on Turn 3!

Takeaway: Whenever human session pauses exceed 5 minutes, an extended 1-hour cache TTL breaks even on Turn 3 and cuts input spend by 64%+ over a 10-turn session.

3. Silent Bill Killer: "Prefix Poisoning" During Deploys

Even with the right TTL, engineering teams frequently hit sudden 3x-8x API bill spikes right after routine backend deployments.

Why? KV prefix caches match exact token byte prefixes from index 0 forward:

  1. system prompt
  2. tools JSON schema array
  3. Conversation history (messages[0..k])

If anything near the top of that sequence mutates between requests or across pods, every downstream token is invalidated. The three most common culprits:

  1. Timestamps or Request Metadata in the System Prompt: Putting Today is 2026-11-12T14:52:09Z or User Tier: Pro | Flags: [beta_v2] at line 1 of the system prompt guarantees a 0% cross-session cache hit rate.
  2. Non-Deterministic Tool Schema Ordering: Dynamically assembling MCP tools or plugin registries from a database query or unordered map (Object.keys()) changes key order across pods, busting the cache for the entire conversation history below it.
  3. Canary / Feature-Flag System Prompt Variants: Rolling out an A/B string tweak inside a 15K-token system prompt splits your warm KV cache across shards.

Fix: Canonical Prefix Normalization (Zero Dependencies)

Move all volatile per-user/per-request context out of the system block and into a structured <runtime_context> block prepended to the latest user turn (the tail of the prompt), and deterministically sort tool definitions before serialization:

interface ToolDef {
  name: string;
  description: string;
  input_schema: Record<string, unknown>;
}

/**
 * Recursively sorts object keys so JSON serialization is byte-identical
 * across Node/Bun/Cloudflare Worker isolates and rolling deploys.
 */
function canonicalizeJson(value: unknown): unknown {
  if (Array.isArray(value)) {
    return value.map(canonicalizeJson);
  }
  if (value !== null && typeof value === 'object') {
    return Object.keys(value as Record<string, unknown>)
      .sort()
      .reduce<Record<string, unknown>>((acc, key) => {
        acc[key] = canonicalizeJson((value as Record<string, unknown>)[key]);
        return acc;
      }, {});
  }
  return value;
}

export function buildCacheSafePayload(params: {
  staticSystemPrompt: string; // Frozen across requests; versioned deliberately
  tools: ToolDef[];
  history: Array<{ role: 'user' | 'assistant'; content: string }>;
  volatileContext: { isoDate: string; userId: string; activeFlags: string[] };
  latestUserPrompt: string;
}) {
  // 1. Deterministic tool ordering + key ordering preserves the KV prefix
  const sortedTools = [...params.tools]
    .sort((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name))
    .map((t) => canonicalizeJson(t) as ToolDef);

  // 2. Volatile metadata lives at the TAIL (never at byte 0 of system prompt)
  const tailContext = [
    `<runtime_context date="${params.volatileContext.isoDate}" flags="${[...params.volatileContext.activeFlags].sort().join(',')}" />`,
    params.latestUserPrompt,
  ].join('\n\n');

  return {
    system: params.staticSystemPrompt,
    tools: sortedTools,
    messages: [
      ...params.history,
      { role: 'user' as const, content: tailContext },
    ],
  };
}

4. Combining Prefix Discipline with 80/20 Tiered Routing

Once your prefix hit rate stabilizes above 85%, adding a lightweight 80/20 intent router compounds the savings:

  • 80% Routine Turns (classification, JSON extraction, CRUD tool calls, short RAG answers): Route to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash ($0.022/$0.40), Qwen 3.8 Flash ($0.15/$0.47), or GPT-6.1 Terra Pro ($1.00/$5.00 with $0.05 cached reads).
  • 20% Hard Reasoning / Architecture Synthesis: Escalate to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or GPT-6.1 Sol Pro ($2.00/$10.00 with $0.10 cached reads)—and validate structured output schemas (Zod / Pydantic) inside your fallback loop so a 200 OK response with malformed JSON automatically retries on the backup provider.

At 10,000 DAU running 15-turn sessions, fixing prefix invalidation plus 80/20 routing routinely drops monthly LLM spend from $18,000+/mo down under $2,900/mo without degrading P95 answer quality.

How are you handling prompt cache invalidation across MCP tool updates or multi-provider fallbacks in production? Drop your architecture patterns in the comments—curious whether more teams are using native provider routing or custom SDK wrappers.

articles.title: 175 MB of Substrings to Read One Column
articles.description: I split a million CSV lines to read one number per row and burned 174 MB of throwaway strings doing it. Here's how Span<Range> splitting dropped that to nothing and ran about twice as fast.
articles.body_html:
I had a boring little job: a pile of CSV-shaped lines in memory, and I needed one number out of each — the amount column, third field, that's it. The rest of the row was along for the ride. I wrote the obvious loop, it gave the right total, and I moved on. Then the allocation profiler lit up on that exact loop and I went back to look. A million rows in, and I'd minted somewhere north of a hundred megabytes of garbage to read a single integer per line. Every other field I split out, I threw straight away.

Here's the loop that did it:

long total = 0;
foreach (string line in lines)
{
    string[] fields = line.Split(',');
    total += long.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
}

line.Split(',') is doing precisely what I asked and nothing I wanted. For each row it allocates a string[] to hold the pieces, then allocates a fresh string for every field it finds, four of them on my data, copying the characters out of the original line into each one. I read fields[2] and let the array and the other three strings fall on the floor. Four columns, five allocations a row, one of them actually used.

The split that doesn't cut anything out

The span-based Split has been around for a couple of versions now and it works on a different idea. Instead of handing you new strings, it tells you where the pieces are. You give it a destination buffer of Range values, it fills in the start and end of each field, and you slice the original line yourself when you want to look at one. Nothing gets copied. Nothing gets allocated.

long total = 0;
Span<Range> ranges = stackalloc Range[8];
foreach (string line in lines)
{
    ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
    int count = span.Split(ranges, ',');
    ReadOnlySpan<char> amount = span[ranges[2]];
    total += long.Parse(amount, CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
}

The stackalloc Range[8] buffer sits on the stack and gets reused on every iteration — one buffer for the whole loop, not one per row. span.Split writes the field boundaries into it and returns how many it found. span[ranges[2]] is a view over the amount field, still pointing into the original line's characters, and long.Parse has had a ReadOnlySpan<char> overload for ages, so it parses that slice straight without a substring in between. The row never becomes an array, the fields never become strings, and the only thing that leaves the loop is the running total.

The numbers

A million rows, built in memory, parsed best-of-7 in a container. Not a lab — I care about the ratio between the two, not the absolute milliseconds on whatever box this ran on.

rows                 : 1,000,000
string.Split sum     : 4,998,543,546
Span<Range> sum      : 4,998,543,546
sums match           : True

string.Split  best   :     75.7 ms   alloc   174.7 MB
Span<Range>   best   :     32.1 ms   alloc     0.0 MB

The sums matching is the part I care about most. Same answer, so this is a fair fight and not a trick where I quietly dropped work. On that footing the span path ran in a bit under half the time and allocated essentially nothing. The 174.7 MB the naive loop burned is all throwaway: arrays and substrings created and collected inside a single pass. Dropping it doesn't just save memory, it saves the GC the job of walking all that back out later, which is a chunk of where the time goes too.

I'll admit I expected the allocation win and only hoped for the speed one. Getting both was the nice surprise.

When I'd leave Split alone

I would not reach for this everywhere, and I'd push back on anyone who tried. If you actually need the fields as strings — you're stashing them in a list, returning them, putting them in a dictionary — then the span version just means you call .ToString() on each slice and you've bought back every allocation you saved, plus more awkward code. The ranges approach pays off exactly when you read the fields, use them, and let them go without keeping them around. Parsing to a number, comparing, summing: yes. Collecting rows into objects you hold onto: no, Split into strings is honest about what you need.

The other caveat is size. At a few hundred rows none of this registers; the naive loop allocates a rounding error and you'd never see it in a profile. This only became worth touching because the row count had three commas and a half-decent chance of growing. Reaching for stackalloc Range[] on a cold path nobody runs in a loop is effort spent making code harder to read for zero measured gain, and I think that trade is a bad one often enough to say it out loud.

One real gotcha: size the Range buffer for the most fields you expect, because Split stops once the destination is full and folds the rest of the line into the last range. Eight slots for four columns gives me headroom; a buffer that's too small turns into a silent correctness bug, not an exception.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself. It's a plain net10.0 console app — one Program.cs, nothing else, build and run with dotnet run -c Release.

using System.Diagnostics;
using System.Globalization;

const int Rows = 1_000_000;
var lines = new string[Rows];
var rng = new Random(42);
string[] regions = ["emea", "apac", "amer", "latam"];
for (int i = 0; i < Rows; i++)
{
    int amount = rng.Next(1, 10_000);
    lines[i] = $"{i},{regions[i & 3]},{amount},{(i % 2 == 0 ? 1 : 0)}";
}

_ = SumWithSplit(lines);   // warm up both paths before timing
_ = SumWithRanges(lines);

const int Trials = 7;
var (splitSum, splitMs, splitBytes) = Measure(() => SumWithSplit(lines), Trials);
var (rangeSum, rangeMs, rangeBytes) = Measure(() => SumWithRanges(lines), Trials);

Console.WriteLine($"sums match        : {splitSum == rangeSum}");
Console.WriteLine($"string.Split  best: {splitMs,8:F1} ms   alloc {splitBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),7:F1} MB");
Console.WriteLine($"Span<Range>   best: {rangeMs,8:F1} ms   alloc {rangeBytes / (1024.0 * 1024.0),7:F1} MB");

static long SumWithSplit(string[] lines)
{
    long total = 0;
    foreach (string line in lines)
    {
        string[] fields = line.Split(',');
        total += long.Parse(fields[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    }
    return total;
}

static long SumWithRanges(string[] lines)
{
    long total = 0;
    Span<Range> ranges = stackalloc Range[8];
    foreach (string line in lines)
    {
        ReadOnlySpan<char> span = line;
        span.Split(ranges, ',');
        total += long.Parse(span[ranges[2]], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture);
    }
    return total;
}

static (long sum, double bestMs, long bytes) Measure(Func<long> work, int trials)
{
    long sum = 0;
    double best = double.MaxValue;
    long bytesForBest = 0;
    for (int t = 0; t < trials; t++)
    {
        GC.Collect();
        GC.WaitForPendingFinalizers();
        GC.Collect();
        long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        sum = work();
        sw.Stop();
        long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
        if (sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds < best)
        {
            best = sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
            bytesForBest = after - before;
        }
    }
    return (sum, best, bytesForBest);
}

Have you swapped a hot Split over to ranges, or found a spot where it wasn't worth the trouble? I'd like to hear where the line fell for you.

— still benchmarking the boring loops nobody asked me to touch

articles.title: "But We Had MFA": A Coffee, a Phishing Story, and Why I'd Bet on Passkeys
articles.description: Every other Friday, I have coffee with a friend who works in IT at a mid-sized company. Usually we...
articles.body_html:
Every other Friday, I have coffee with a friend who works in IT at a mid-sized company. Usually we talk about football, side projects, and which framework will be dead next year.

Last time, my friend sat down, didn't even touch the cup, and said:

"We got phished. And we had MFA."

Then, after a pause: "I don't get it. We did everything right."

That conversation lasted two hours and three coffees. I ended up drawing on a napkin. On the way home I thought: if a smart IT person is this confused, a lot of people must be. So here's the napkin, cleaned up.

What happened

Someone in their accounting team got an email: "A shared invoice is waiting, sign in to view it." The link opened a page that looked exactly like their Microsoft login. Same logo, same font, same little loading dots.

She typed her password. Then she received an SMS code, a real one, from her real company, and typed that too.

Twenty seconds later, the attacker was in her mailbox. They set up a rule forwarding every invoice to a Gmail address. That's how IT noticed, two days later.

"She didn't do anything stupid," my friend kept saying. And that's the point. She didn't.

Napkin #1: the page wasn't fake, it was a mirror

The first thing I drew was this:

This is called AiTM phishing (Adversary-in-the-Middle). The fake page doesn't just store your password. It sits between you and the real login page and forwards everything, live. The real server sees a perfectly valid login: right password, right code. And it hands the session cookie over to the attacker.

"So our MFA was useless?" my friend asked.

Not useless. It blocks the attacker who bought a list of leaked passwords. It doesn't block someone relaying your login in real time. Those kits are sold as a service now, with a monthly subscription and customer support. You don't need to be a genius to run one.

The rule I wrote under the drawing: anything a human can type, a human can type in the wrong place.

Napkin #2: "Should we switch from SAML to OIDC?"

That was the next question. Their security consultant had mentioned OIDC was "more modern", someone else wanted to replace SMS with an authenticator app, and it was all getting mixed up.

So I drew a nightclub. 🎟️

  • The bouncer checks your ID at the door. That's authentication: are you really you? Password, OTP, fingerprint... these are the ways the bouncer checks.
  • Once you're in, you get a wristband. Every bar inside trusts it, nobody checks your ID again. That's federation. SAML and OIDC are two kinds of wristband.
  • The front desk that checks IDs and hands out wristbands is the IdP (Identity Provider).

"So SAML versus OTP is a nonsense question," my friend said. Exactly. One is the wristband, the other is the ID check. You need both, and switching wristbands doesn't fix a bouncer who can be fooled.

SAML, the old wristband (2005)

XML. The IdP sends your app a signed document: "this is Alice, finance group, valid for 5 minutes." It usually travels through the browser as an auto-submitted form.

It's everywhere in big companies and it works. But verifying XML signatures correctly is hard. In 2024 and 2025, ruby-saml (behind GitLab's SAML login, among others) had critical bugs where two XML parsers read the same document differently, letting an attacker log in as anyone.

My advice: SAML is fine, as long as you never write your own parser.

OIDC, the new wristband (2014)

Built on OAuth 2.0. JSON and JWT instead of XML. It's what's behind "Sign in with Google", and it's much nicer for SPAs, mobile apps and APIs.

For anything new: Authorization Code flow + PKCE. If a tutorial tells you to use the "implicit flow" and grab the token from the URL, close the tab. It's deprecated, and OAuth 2.1 drops it.

OTP, one way of checking IDs

Authenticator apps (TOTP), HOTP, SMS, email codes. It's a factor, not a protocol. It made stolen passwords far less useful, and I won't bash it.

But as my friend's accountant learned: an OTP is a second password that expires quickly. Quick enough to beat a leaked database. Not quick enough to beat a live relay.

SAML 2.0 OIDC OTP
Nightclub version Old wristband New wristband One way to check your ID
What it is Federation protocol Federation protocol Authentication factor
Format Signed XML JSON / JWT 6-digit code
Good for Enterprise SSO, legacy apps Web, SPA, mobile, APIs Second factor
Classic trap Signature validation bugs Wildcard redirects, tokens in localStorage Phishing, SIM swap

Napkin #3: "We have logins everywhere"

Then my friend admitted the other problem. After the incident, they listed every internal app with a login. There were way more than they expected. Some used the company SSO, some had their own users table, and changing a rule meant touching each one.

That's where an IdP like Keycloak makes sense. It's open source, it speaks SAML and OIDC, so old apps keep SAML and new ones use OIDC, on the same SSO session. It plugs into an existing Active Directory, so nobody recreates their account. And when an account is compromised, you disable it once and every session dies, everywhere.

To try it in five minutes:

docker run -p 8080:8080 \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME=admin \
  -e KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD=admin \
  quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:latest start-dev

(Pin a real version in production. latest in prod is how you get surprised on a Friday.)

I told my friend: the first thing I'd check in any setup is the redirect URIs. If you see this, fix it today:

"redirectUris": ["*"]

A wildcard means anyone can ask the IdP to send the authorization code to their site. Here's what a SPA client should look like:

{
  "clientId": "my-spa",
  "publicClient": true,
  "standardFlowEnabled": true,
  "implicitFlowEnabled": false,
  "directAccessGrantsEnabled": false,
  "redirectUris": ["https://app.example.com/callback"],
  "webOrigins": ["https://app.example.com"],
  "attributes": {
    "pkce.code.challenge.method": "S256"
  }
}

No implicit flow. No password grant (your app should never see the user's password). Exact redirect URIs. PKCE required. That's 80% of the job.

Napkin #4: the one my friend didn't believe

"Fine," my friend said, "but even with Keycloak, the mirror page can still relay a password and a code."

True. Centralizing doesn't fix that. So I said the word: passkeys.

The look I got was the same look I get from everyone: "No password at all? That sounds like less security."

I get it. It sounds like removing the lock. It's actually replacing it with one that can't be picked.

In plain words: when you register a passkey, your phone or laptop creates two keys. The private one never leaves your device. The server only keeps the public one. When you log in, the server sends a challenge, your device signs it after you touch the fingerprint sensor or look at the camera, and the server checks the signature.

And here's what would have saved the accountant: a passkey is tied to the real domain. On login-micros0ft-secure.com, the browser simply won't offer it. No code to type, nothing to relay. The mirror page gets nothing.

Bonus: if the database leaks, the attacker gets a pile of public keys. Useless.

Keycloak supports it natively. Roughly (menu names move a bit between versions):

  1. Authentication → Policies → WebAuthn Passwordless Policy: set User Verification Requirement to required.
  2. Duplicate the browser flow and add the WebAuthn Passwordless authenticator.
  3. Enable the Webauthn Register Passwordless required action, so people enroll at their next login.
  4. Bind the new flow to the realm.

My advice: start with the team that got hit. Offer passkeys next to the password first, then make them mandatory for the sensitive roles.

The text I got three weeks later

My friend texted me a screenshot of their Keycloak config, then: "Finance is on passkeys. The guy who complained the most now asks why the other tools don't do it."

Then, a week after: "Our CTO dropped his phone in a lake. Only passkey. Locked out. 🙃"

That's the last thing I want you to take from this post. Once you go passwordless, attackers move to "I lost my device." If your recovery process is "call support and give your date of birth", you've just moved the front door to the helpdesk. And attackers are very good on the phone, now with AI-cloned voices too.

What I suggested:

  • everyone registers at least two passkeys (phone + laptop, or a hardware key in a drawer),
  • recovery is as strict as login: identity check, a delay, a notification to the user,
  • the helpdesk has one rule: never reset a factor based on a phone call alone. Even if it sounds like the CEO. Especially if it sounds like the CEO.

The CTO got back in. He now has a YubiKey on his keychain, and apparently mentions it in every meeting.

What I'd want you to remember

SAML and OIDC pass your identity between apps. OTP is one way to check it. An IdP like Keycloak puts it all in one place you can actually control.

But the attacks that hurt today don't crack anything. They impersonate. And against impersonation, the only factors that hold are the ones with nothing to type into the wrong page.

My friend's company had MFA. They still got phished. If you're still sending SMS codes to your users, no judgment, most of us are. But maybe put "try passkeys" in your next sprint before you need a coffee like that one.

Details changed to keep my friend's company anonymous. Did you roll out passkeys? Did someone on your team also drop their phone in a lake? Tell me in the comments.

You've watched the Git tutorial.

You nodded along. Everything made sense.

Then you hit your first merge conflict at work and froze. 🥶

I've been there. That's exactly why I built GitMission.

Tutorials give you a false sense of progress

Watching someone run git rebase feels like learning.

It isn't.

Here's what usually happens:

  • You follow along while the video is playing
  • You close the tab
  • A week later, you can't remember the commands Your brain learned to recognize Git. It never learned to use it.

Those are two very different skills.

Git is learned with your fingers, not your eyes

Think about the last thing you got good at.

Did you get good by watching, or by doing, failing, and trying again?

Git works the same way. You need to:

  • Type the commands
  • Break things on purpose
  • Fix what you broke That's the loop that makes it stick.

Take the Git skills test

So I built a place where you can break things safely

GitMission is an interactive Git platform that runs entirely in your browser.

No install. No setup. No fear of wrecking a real repo.

Here's what you get:

  • 🖥️ A real in-browser Git terminal with instant feedback on every command
  • ✏️ A built-in code editor, so you practice the full flow from edit to commit
  • 👥 A virtual engineering team that assigns tasks, sets context, and puts you in realistic situations
  • 🎯 Real-world scenarios like merge conflicts, messy rebases, and recovering lost commits Here's the kind of thing you'll see in a mission: 
Marcus (Senior Dev): Before I pick up the login work,
can you print the commits made so far?

$ git log --oneline

No multiple choice. You type the command. The platform checks it.

"But I just use AI to write my code..."

Let's talk about vibe coders. 👀

AI can write your features in minutes. That's amazing.

But AI also:

  • Rewrites files you didn't ask it to touch
  • Introduces bugs you won't notice until later
  • Makes big changes in a single shot Without Git, you have no undo button.

With Git, you can:

  • ✅ Commit a working state before every AI experiment
  • ✅ See exactly what the AI changed with git diff
  • ✅ Roll back with git revert or git reset when things go sideways
  • ✅ Branch off and try risky ideas without touching main The faster you build, the more you need a safety net.

Vibe coding without Git is driving fast with no brakes.

Git is not optional if you want a dev job

Almost every software team uses Git.

It's not a "nice to have" on a resume. It's assumed.

In interviews, you'll often be asked about:

  • Branching and merging
  • Rebasing vs merging
  • Resolving conflicts

  • Undoing mistakes
    And on day one of a real job, you'll be expected to:

  • Create a branch for your task

  • Open a pull request

  • Respond to code review
    Knowing the definitions isn't enough.

You need experience, so your answers come from something you've actually done.

8 missions. About 7 hours of hands-on practice. Zero fluff.

1. Introduction to Git What Git is and how to set it up
2. Tracking Changes init, status, add, commit

5. Branching create, switch, merge, delete
6. Advanced Git stash, rebase, cherry-pick, bisect
7. GitHub Basics SSH keys, push, pull, clone
8. Advanced GitHub & Collaboration forks, pull requests, code reviews

Start at the beginning, or jump straight to the scary stuff like rebase and conflicts.

  • 🤖 Vibe coders who want a safety net for AI-generated code
  • 💼 Job seekers preparing for interviews and their first dev role

Before you start learning, find out where you stand.

I made a free Git skills test:

  • 30 questions
  • 20 seconds each
  • 3 difficulty levels, from beginner to advanced
  • No signup, no install You also get a topic-by-topic breakdown and explanations for every wrong answer.

Think you'll ace it? 😏

👉 Take the Git skills test

Drop your score in the comments. I'm curious who gets 30/30. 👇

Ready to start?

Your first mission needs no login and no credit card.

The Git fundamentals are free to try. The advanced missions are unlocked with Pro, which is a one-time purchase, not a subscription.

Final thought

You don't learn Git by watching someone else use it.

You learn it by getting stuck, fixing it, and doing it again.

That's the whole idea behind GitMission.

articles.title: Shipping in-browser WASM background removal without crashing Safari tabs (+ an open real-device latency dataset)
articles.description: Over the past month I built and shipped remove.ac, an image background remover split into two...
articles.body_html:
Over the past month I built and shipped remove.ac, an image background remover split into two explicit execution paths: a free in-browser WebAssembly studio where image bytes stay inside the tab, and an optional stateless Cloud GPU API (POST /v1.0/removebg) compatible with remove.bg payloads.

Running a 1024px segmentation model (onnxruntime-web WASM + guided-filter hair refinement) inside real users' browsers surfaced a few bugs that never showed up on an M-series MacBook during development. Here is what broke, how we fixed it, and the raw telemetry we collected from 2,000+ production runs.

1. WebKit holds onto offscreen <canvas> memory after unmount

Dropping references to temporary <canvas> elements in React was enough in Chromium, but iOS and macOS Safari kept hundreds of megabytes of backing-store memory pinned across batch runs. Explicitly zeroing dimensions (canvas.width = 0; canvas.height = 0) in teardown routines reclaimed memory immediately and stopped mobile tab reloads during 50-image ZIP batches on /batch.

2. Bounding manual brush undo history to 64 MB

On a 12 MP product photo, storing 10 undo snapshots as raw RGBA ImageData eats ~480 MB on its own. For the local Erase / Restore / Smart Brush and point/box subject selector, we switched to replaying stroke vectors on top of a rolling checkpoint canvas, capping undo history at 12 steps within a 64 MB ceiling.

3. Never silently fall back from local WASM to a backend server

A subtle trust bug in "hybrid" web tools is catching an out-of-memory WASM error and quietly uploading the file to a cloud worker so the task succeeds. If someone picked on-device processing for an ID scan or unreleased product shot, silent fallback violates the whole point. On remove.ac, local failures stay local; Cloud GPU runs only when a signed-in user clicks it or calls the API with an X-Api-Key (rac_live_...).

4. Bypassing serverless ~4 MB gateway caps without storing user files on S3

Standard serverless HTTP gateways choke around 4.5 MB, which fails as soon as a studio photographer outputs a 15 MB lossless PNG. Instead of staging uploads in an object bucket, our zero-dependency SDKs and CLI request a single-use HMAC ticket from POST /v1.0/removebg/ticket (placing a Postgres FEFO credit hold) and stream up to 25 MB / 40 MP directly into volatile GPU worker RAM. If inference errors out or times out, the credit hold releases automatically at zero cost.

Open SDKs (MIT) and Real-Device Latency Dataset (CC BY 4.0)

  • Zero-dependency Node.js & Python SDKs + --watch folder CLI: github.com/szp2005/remove-ac-sdk (includes a 1-line from removebg import RemoveBg drop-in shim).
  • Rolling 90-day real-device WASM benchmark dataset: remove.ac/benchmarks — publishes p50/p95 download, session-init, and inference timings across desktop/mobile CPU buckets (raw JSON and CSV under CC BY 4.0, no cherry-picked single-machine numbers).

If you want to poke at the browser WASM studio (no login wall) or test /v1.0/removebg with the free signup credit, everything is live at https://remove.ac. Happy to share details on the guided-filter worker pipeline or the Postgres FEFO ledger SQL!

articles.title: AI is getting better. Here is my plan to stay ahead.
articles.description: AI is getting better every day.  As a software engineer, this is a topic that is often top of mind,...
articles.body_html:
AI is getting better every day.

As a software engineer, this is a topic that is often top of mind, which prompted me to share the plan I've put into action to keep an edge over AI.

I believe it is a useful trait to be paranoid, within reason.

Leveraging new tools and technologies to remain relevant is arguably the nature of our job.

Disclaimer that this is not a plan to save the world (I wish I had all the answers!) but rather my personal set of actions I believe will increase my odds of maintaining an edge over AI.

At least for a little while longer...

Here is a visualization of my plan. We will cover each part in detail.

Foundations and fundamentals

Before we dive into my actual plan, let's start with a short story.

The story of how I became a software engineer.

If someone had told me 10 years ago that I would be working as a software engineer today, I would not have believed them.

I was at university studying business and finance.

After graduating, I started interviewing for jobs in finance. In parallel, I was experimenting with drones, which were a hobby of mine.

I quickly realized that there was an opportunity to package drone services to realtors to promote their luxury properties via aerial imagery and video.

I learned a lot in the process from cold calling, marketing, financial planning and account management.

But above all, I learned that I wanted to build software. We had clients asking us for tools to edit our media assets, store, stream and serve them to their clients. This got me digging into the internals of software and opened my eyes to numerous possibilities.

Shortly after, I signed up to a coding bootcamp to learn web development fundamentals.

I struggled during 9 intensive weeks, but it was transformative in the best way possible.

My brain was challenged to think in new ways: data structures and patterns, software design and components, principles and frameworks.

I haven't stopped coding since.

6 years of building software, from startups to larger companies.

I recently started a new job as a software engineer and noticed how my ways of working have drastically changed since my first lines of professional code.

I am not saying things are better or worse.

Just like my irregular path, each step brings along its set of challenges but also rewards.

Change is the only constant, and with it come boundless opportunities.

I wanted to open with my story to encourage you to embrace change and also emphasize the importance of investing in fundamentals.

This is foundational to what we will cover in the next parts.

Unlock potential with the right mindset

An optimistic mindset is key to unlocking potential and working alongside AI in a positive way.

In some cases, there is too much pessimism surrounding AI.

I don't believe this is healthy.

I am not saying we should blindly trust AI, but we should accept it as new tooling that can be leveraged and start getting used to it as a new norm.

I acknowledge that the job market is tough, especially for junior developers.

Stay curious, passionate, excited, open-minded.

Within my network, I have witnessed juniors with no professional experience be very creative and resourceful, and land great professional opportunities.

I highly recommend reading the post Hunger Beats Tenure written by Felix Rieseberg, a leading engineer at Anthropic. The post conveys a refreshingly optimistic take for junior developers with practical actions to take to stand out in the current job market such as leaning into your fresh perspective and aiming for radical ideas with big potential for change.

Pick a development plan and stick to it

Think hard about your personal goals and build a development plan to reach them.

In this attention economy, people tend to swipe from one thing to the next, chasing one hot topic after another.

There is no harm in staying on top of industry trends. However don't make this your core strategy.

This age of AI rewards both generalists and specialists. The former can create associations across tools nobody has considered and the latter can unlock deep intuitions.

I personally like to follow a T-shaped development approach to get the best of both worlds.

The horizontal bar of the T represents my efforts to stay on top of the latest trends and experiment, whilst the vertical stem of the T is me deepening my knowledge within fintech engineering. This is where I spend most of my learning and development time (70-80%).

Follow your plan rigorously. It might feel slow at the start but once you pick up momentum you will feel the benefits when the dots start to connect.

Deepen domain expertise

My focus is on deepening my knowledge within one specific domain to gain invaluable experience and industry knowledge that will make you stand out from the crowd.

If you can combine deep knowledge at a business level and translate that knowledge into technical solutions, you will be perceived as unique and valuable.

In my case, I am developing an edge as a fintech engineer.

I have been working in the space for almost 5 years now and understand how payment flows and systems work under the hood.

I stay on top of the latest trends through various resources such as books borrowed from my local library, podcasts and newsletters and through community meetups.

If you are interested in fintech, I personally recommend the following books as a start:

  • The Anatomy of the Swipe
  • The Pay Off

Broaden your awareness of tools

Become AI-native, not AI-dependent.

Know when to leverage AI appropriately by making use of available tooling.

AI is powerful for information retrieval, exploration and synthesis.

In this sense, context management becomes critical.

Here are some practices that have helped me work more effectively with AI:

  • invest more time upfront gathering requirements and discussing requirements with stakeholders, and collecting these findings in a living document your agent can ingest
  • embrace spec-driven development to structure your AI output
  • invest your time writing detailed Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to capture the why not just the what
  • connect your tools and sources of information through MCP servers and connectors to plug your agent across all critical tools (Jira, GitHub, Slack, etc.)
  • explore broadly with AI before going deep with your judgment
  • use AI to be more proactive with stakeholders by sharing prototypes rather than just documents to convey ideas better
  • leverage AI to be more helpful to others. For example, last week I used Claude to generate a Go guide for my team's onboarding

Minimize AI slop

Leveraging AI is good, but using it deliberately is even better.

Just because AI makes it easier to produce more doesn't mean you should.

When joining a new organization, don't jump in and make changes immediately.

Learn the engineering ways of working first before making any changes.

With AI-driven development, if you don't understand the rules and define scope, the blast radius can be high.

Some practices I adopt at work:

  • scope PRs to smaller changes to make reviews easier and limit potential issues
  • think before prompting by writing down your thoughts, assumptions and approach
  • introduce human checkpoints (architectural decisions, big change reviews)
  • when prompting, define your target audience to increase relevancy

Before sharing AI-generated work, I ask myself:

  • Have I actually reviewed it? A simple rule should be: don't share a document with others that you wouldn't read yourself
  • Am I contributing original thinking? Personal insights, experiences, perspectives.
  • Am I saving people time or costing them time? A lengthy AI-generated document can take minutes to generate but take hours for colleagues to interpret.
  • Am I confident signing my name on the AI work? Accountability is key.
  • Am I using an AI disclaimer? Explicitly mention when an artifact is AI-generated so consumers can apply extra scrutiny when reviewing.

An informal way of measuring the above is to ask yourself: are you someone people enjoy working with who provides value?

You can go a step further and drive value at an organizational level.

From experience, AI is not good at driving change at that level effectively and with positive feedback from engineers.

AI tends to overengineer. I always appreciate an engineering culture that solves complex problems with simple solutions and effective tooling.

Personality beats information

With information becoming increasingly accessible, personality, experiences and unique perspectives become more valuable.

I invest more time in developing my soft skills that make me a better collaborator:

  • communication
  • listening
  • gathering requirements

People tend to value an experience more than just the solution.

This post on X conveys this idea nicely:

Don't let AI take away your opinions, the fun and joy of building.

I never stop building and experimenting.

I've noticed that more companies seem to recognize that in the age of AI, a strong recruiting signal is whether the candidate can entertain a passionate discussion about building software systems.

Passion and excitement are behind the best software. This contributes to the experience provided.

Instead of beating AI at what it does best, I try to beat it where it performs worse: passionate and creative thinking derived from real-world experiences and unique perspectives.

I spend time building my network. To be part of a community that challenges and sharpens my perspectives.

AI can't replace the raw sharing of human experiences.

I actually attended a meetup the other week with the theme 'What can't AI do?'

Amongst fellow engineers, we spent hours debating and sharing our unique perspectives.

I aim to elevate and share my unique voice.

To build a personal identity and contribute to the conversation.

Some ways this can be done:

  • write on DEV by sharing your experiments, thoughts and discoveries
  • engage on LinkedIn and connect with others
  • maintain a portfolio of projects on GitHub that reflect who you are and what you are passionate about

It is not only the what you are building that is important; it is the why.

My question to you is: are you also working on your own plan? Which skills are you currently investing in?

If so, I would love to know more! Please share any useful tips with the community on how you are maintaining an edge over AI.

If not, it is not too late to start working on one! Let me know in the comments if you require any advice, I would be happy to help you get started.

articles.body_html:
So, why should I bring this up again?

Because Qoder (Alibaba’s AI IDE) free promo has officially ended (@unitbuilds, 😢), and now that I’m left with only free browser-based AI, I finally have time to actually test my extension and fix a few friction points.

Before going into the updates, let me show you how ReptClip works as simply as possible, with screen recordings along the way! 🙂

How it works

It's a 3-step process. Ideally, put VS Code and your free chatbot side-by-side.

Step 1: Copy context to clipboard

Specify the files you want to include in the context. You can use relative paths or glob patterns. Press "Enter" or click the "Generate" button to copy the context straight to your clipboard.

Besides the files you specify, the context also includes the project structure and instructions on how to generate the output. You can enable/disable each section using checkboxes.

Step 2: Paste context into your chatbot, along with your prompt

Send it and let it generate.

Step 3: Apply the generated diffs

The chatbot will provide the diffs in a single code block. Copy them, and click "Apply Diffs" to apply them.

Optional step (before step 3): Add more files to the context

If the chatbot wants to see more files, it will generate a code block containing the relative paths of the files. You can copy that block and click the "More Files" button to copy the contents of those files only to the clipboard, and paste it back to the chatbot.

A little behind-the-scenes: Every animated WebP you see above was captured, edited, and exported using GiffyPy, an all-in-one screen recording and video editing tool that I built myself!

So, that's basically what the extension does! A few other features:

  • Live syntax highlighting and autocomplete
  • Fuzzy diff matching
  • All-or-nothing diff application to prevent partial or broken edits
  • Session undo/redo for the last 10 diffs
  • Warning before re-applying the same diff
  • .gitignore enforcement & binary/size guards (skips ignored, binary, or large files)
  • Per-project persistent settings & custom defaults through settings
  • And more! (check out the README for full details)

Updates

I updated the UI to save space, added settings to customize default project UI state, and added undo/redo functionality. Now it's very usable in my opinion!

Feedback corner

So, what do you think about this extension? Is it good? Would you install this extension in your IDE? It's available in both the VS Code Marketplace and the Open VSX Registry. So you can install it in VSCodium, Cursor, Windsurf, Devin Desktop, Qoder, etc. as well!

  • ReptClip Official GitHub repository (source available!)
  • VS Code Marketplace
  • Open VSX Registry

I'd be sooo sooo grateful if you could star the repo! Please do it 🥰

articles.title: Codex Never Crashed. It Just Quietly Did Nothing.
articles.description: From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents...
articles.body_html:
Codex Never Crashed. It Just Quietly Did Nothing.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is journal Group 21 of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

Three bugs stood between me and a live Codex CLI integration. Not one of them printed an error. Every one of them let my harness sit there looking finished while producing nothing. This is the kind of debugging session that makes you stop trusting a quiet process.

Trap one: the API you assumed still exists

I wired Codex CLI against my local model server the way I had wired everything else: chat completions, the endpoint every OpenAI-compatible server speaks. Codex refused at startup: wire_api = "chat" is no longer supported. The CLI dropped chat completions entirely. The only transport it accepts now is the OpenAI Responses API.

The lesson is not "read the changelog," although yes. The lesson is that my local server, oMLX, happened to serve /v1/responses natively, and I only found that out with a curl probe instead of an assumption. One probe, a real resp_* body, HTTP 200. The entire integration unblocked with zero translation layers.

Vendor APIs drift. Probe the transport fresh for every CLI-to-endpoint pairing, every CLI version. Yesterday's working config is today's silent startup rejection.

Trap two: the stdin hang

codex exec, run headless from a test script, printed "Reading additional input from stdin..." and then sat there. No error. No timeout. No exit. My harness, which was watching the process and its output, looked "busy." The run produced zero evidence and appeared, from a process list, to be working.

The cause: codex exec reads stdin, and in a harness stdin is whatever the parent left connected, which is never a closing TTY. The fix is two characters of shell: </dev/null. Close stdin by default in every headless invocation.

This one deserves a rule of its own: any headless CLI that consumes stdin will hang your harness quietly. An unattended process with a blocked read is the most patient bug in the world. It will wait forever, and your CI will show a spinner.

Trap three: the 404s that blamed the server

With transport sorted and stdin closed, every model call returned 404. Uniform, instant 404s. I spent a while on the server side, checking routes, because 404 says "server problem," right?

Codex appends /responses to the provider base_url I configured. My proxy URL was http://127.0.0.1:PORT, so Codex called /responses. The server serves /v1/responses. The fix: base_url = "http://127.0.0.1:PORT/v1". Off by one suffix, every call dead, server completely healthy the whole time.

Paths are config. Config is a test surface. A uniform 404 across every request is almost never "the server is broken." It is "the client is asking somewhere else."

The honest scoping problem

There was a fourth decision, not a bug, a design call. Claude Code has a pausable per-call approval hook. I could wire the policy engine directly into the ask-a-human loop and test it live. Codex, headless, does not. Its governance surface is the sandbox and the config file: --sandbox read-only, provider config, executed commands.

I could have forced parity and written a fake approval flow. Instead the case tests what the surface actually guarantees. Allow means the command executed, a real cat that printed real output. Deny means the destructive command was blocked, the target directory stayed intact with its keep.txt, and the agent replanned. Plus a parity check: the same three commands decided by the engine before execution, with an audit file showing allow, escalate, deny matching the in-process engine exactly.

A harness test should assert what the surface guarantees and say so out loud. Stretching a different harness's shape over a vendor surface produces tests that pass and prove nothing.

The final wiring, for the record

Codex CLI 0.135.0 against the box-local model, no OpenAI key. A stdlib logging proxy (t1_proxy.py) between the CLI and the model server captured 4 request and 4 response pairs, sanitized, all 2xx. The parity audit trail has 3 decisions. The allow executed, the deny held and replanned, and the whole thing reproduces from the committed config (t1_codex.sh, codex-home/config.toml in the case's evidence directory).

What worked

  • Probing before wiring. The Responses API question was settled with one curl before any config existed.
  • Capturing LLM traffic as a hard requirement. Every pair on disk or the case fails. That rule is the only reason "looked busy, did nothing" runs got caught at all.
  • Testing the pieces standalone before composing them: policy through evaluate first, then the proxy with curl, then the CLI through the proxy. Each failure lived in exactly one layer.

What did not work

  • Trusting that chat completions would still be the transport. It was not, and finding out cost me a full debug cycle.
  • Leaving stdin connected. Obvious in hindsight, invisible in the process list.
  • Reading 404 as "server broken" before reading it as "client asking in the wrong place."

More detail and evidence

  • The full Codex story: field test report, journal Group 21 (FT-T1-CODEX), plus Field Notes 12 for the write-up version of the same traps.
  • The harness, in the repo: t1_codex.sh (config, parity triple, sandbox triple) · t1_proxy.py (the /responses-aware capture proxy) · t1_policy.yaml (the shared Tier-1 policy).
  • The captured evidence: field-test/v0.1.0/results/s18-tier1/cases/FT-T1-CODEX/ in the repo (live transcripts, audit trail, 4 LLM pairs, provider config).
  • The plan row that scoped the case honestly: FIELD_TEST_PLAN.md, the FT-T1-CODEX row and the Tier-1 R-map.
  • The product: agentpolicy, pip install agentsec-agentpolicy, PyPI 0.1.0, docs reference (adapters, authzen, surfaces), part of the agentic-suite agent-security stack.

What is the most patient bug you have shipped in a harness? The one that produced no output, no error, and no exit, just quiet nothing. I want to know I am not alone.

articles.title: 10 AI Prompts Every Developer Should Know
articles.description: I think most developers are underusing AI.  Not because they don't know which tools to use.  Not...
articles.body_html:
I think most developers are underusing AI.

Not because they don't know which tools to use.

Not because they haven't tried the latest coding assistants.

And certainly not because they don't know how to write prompts.

The problem is something more interesting.

We're using incredibly powerful AI systems to answer questions that are often too vague to be useful.

Think about how developers commonly interact with AI:

"Write this function."

"Fix this bug."

"Optimize this code."

"Explain this error."

"Make this application better."

These instructions aren't necessarily wrong.

But they leave almost everything important to interpretation.

What constraints should the AI consider?

What would a successful result look like?

What assumptions is it making?

How should we verify its suggestions?

After spending years exploring AI and prompt engineering, I've become increasingly convinced of one thing:

The quality of an AI-assisted development workflow depends less on clever wording and more on how clearly we define the task.

So here are ten prompts I believe every developer should keep handy.

They're not magic commands. They're reusable starting points for better engineering.

1. The Requirement Clarifier

When to use: Before writing code for a new feature.

One of the most expensive mistakes in software development is implementing a requirement nobody properly understood.

Instead of immediately asking AI to generate a solution, ask it to examine the problem.

Prompt:

I am planning to build the following feature:
[Describe the feature]
Act as a requirements reviewer.
Before suggesting an implementation:
1. Identify ambiguous requirements.
2. List missing information.
3. Identify important edge cases.
4. Separate assumptions from confirmed facts.
5. Suggest measurable acceptance criteria.
6. Ask the five most important questions I should answer before development.

Do not generate code yet.

Why is this useful?

Because it moves the difficult questions to the beginning of the development process.

You might discover that a supposedly simple feature contains several decisions nobody has made.

The best time to discover an incomplete requirement is before you've built the solution.

2. The Architecture Challenger

When to use: Before choosing frameworks, services, or infrastructure.

Developers can easily fall into a familiar trap.

We discover an interesting technology and start looking for an opportunity to use it.

But good architecture should begin with the problem, not the tool.

Prompt:

I need to build a system that does the following:

[Describe the problem]

Constraints:
- Expected users: [Number]
- Expected traffic: [Volume]
- Team size: [Size]
- Budget: [Budget]
- Existing stack: [Technologies]

Propose the simplest architecture that meets these requirements.

Then:

1. Explain the main components and data flow.
2. Identify potential failure points.
3. Explain what should remain simple.
4. Identify unnecessary abstractions.
5. Compare it with one reasonable alternative.
6. Explain when the alternative would become a better choice.

Optimize for maintainability and reliability, not technological sophistication.

I especially like the last instruction.

AI can suggest impressive architectures.

But an impressive architecture isn't necessarily an appropriate one.

Sometimes a single application is better than five microservices.

Sometimes a deterministic workflow is better than an autonomous agent.

I've explored this distinction in Stop Building AI Agents. Start Building AI Systems.

The goal is not to build the most sophisticated system. It's to build the right system.

3. The Codebase Explorer

When to use: When joining a new project or working with unfamiliar code.

Understanding an existing application can be harder than writing new code.

You need to understand not only what the functions do, but also how the components interact.

Prompt:

I am trying to understand this codebase.

Here are the relevant files and project details:

[Provide files, snippets, and folder structure]

Help me understand:

1. The main responsibilities of each component.
2. The entry points and execution flow.
3. How data moves between components.
4. Important dependencies.
5. Where errors are handled.
6. Which files I should study first.

Explain the system from the perspective of a developer who needs to modify it safely.

Do not assume missing files or behavior. Clearly identify anything you cannot verify.

That final instruction matters.

AI sometimes fills gaps with plausible explanations.

But a plausible explanation is not the same as understanding the actual codebase.

I want the model to tell me when it doesn't know something.

Not invent the missing architecture.

4. The Controlled Code Generator

When to use: When you want AI to implement a clearly defined feature.

AI-generated code can save enormous amounts of time.

But unrestricted code generation may introduce unnecessary dependencies, abstractions, or unrelated changes.

Prompt:

Implement the following feature:

[Feature description]

Existing code:
[Relevant code]

Requirements:
[Acceptance criteria]

Constraints:
- Language/framework: [Stack]
- Files allowed to change: [Files]
- Dependencies: [Allowed dependencies]
- Compatibility: [Requirements]

Instructions:

1. Make the smallest reasonable change.
2. Preserve existing behavior unless specified.
3. Do not introduce unnecessary abstractions.
4. Do not invent APIs or dependencies.
5. Explain important implementation decisions.
6. Include relevant tests.
7. List assumptions and anything that still requires verification.

Provide the implementation and a summary of the changes.

Notice that we're not simply asking:

"Write the code."

We're defining the boundaries within which the code should be written.

That's closer to how good engineering teams communicate tasks.

Constraints often improve the usefulness of AI-generated code.

5. The Debugging Investigator

When to use: When something breaks and the cause isn't obvious.

This is one of my favorite ways to use AI.

Instead of asking it to fix a bug immediately, ask it to investigate the problem.

Prompt:

I am debugging an issue.

Expected behavior:
[What should happen]

Actual behavior:
[What happens]

Error messages:
[Logs or errors]

Relevant code:
[Code]

Steps to reproduce:
[Steps]

Act as a debugging investigator.

1. Identify the most likely causes.
2. Rank them by likelihood and available evidence.
3. Explain which observations support each cause.
4. Suggest the next diagnostic test.
5. Explain what each test result would tell us.
6. Recommend a fix only after identifying a sufficiently supported root cause.

Do not present hypotheses as established facts.

Why do I prefer this?

Because debugging is not simply changing code until the error disappears.

It's understanding why the problem exists.

A suggested fix might eliminate the visible symptom while leaving the underlying problem untouched.

AI should help us investigate the bug, not simply guess at the solution.

6. The Test Case Designer

When to use: Before merging a feature or releasing a change.

Developers often test the behavior they expect.

But unexpected behavior is where many interesting bugs hide.

AI can be useful for expanding our thinking about test coverage.

Prompt:

Review the following function or feature:

[Code or feature description]

Expected behavior:
[Requirements]

Design a comprehensive test plan covering:

1. Normal inputs.
2. Boundary conditions.
3. Empty or missing values.
4. Invalid inputs.
5. Failure scenarios.
6. Duplicate requests or retries.
7. Relevant security edge cases.
8. Important regression cases.

For each test, provide:
- The scenario.
- The input.
- The expected result.
- Why the test matters.

Then generate tests using [Framework].

Do not assume that existing behavior is correct. Identify unclear expectations separately.

The instruction about existing behavior is particularly important.

If the implementation already contains a bug, generating tests that merely reproduce its behavior can reinforce the mistake.

We want tests based on intended requirements.

Not just tests that agree with the code.

For a deeper discussion of this problem, I wrote Most Developers Test Their Code. Why Don't They Test Their AI?.

7. The Critical Code Reviewer

When to use: Before submitting or approving a pull request.

Here's where I believe AI becomes especially useful.

Not as a replacement for human code review, but as another perspective.

Prompt:

Review this code as a critical software engineer.

[Code or diff]

Project context:
[Relevant requirements and architecture]

Evaluate it for:

1. Correctness.
2. Missing edge cases.
3. Security risks.
4. Error handling.
5. Maintainability.
6. Unnecessary complexity.
7. Backward compatibility.
8. Missing tests.

For each finding:

- Describe the specific issue.
- Explain its potential impact.
- Assign a severity level.
- Reference the relevant code.
- Suggest the smallest reasonable improvement.

Separate confirmed defects from possible risks.

Do not rewrite the entire implementation unless a broader redesign is justified.

This avoids one of the problems I frequently see in AI-assisted coding.

A developer asks for a review.

The AI immediately generates an entirely new implementation.

But perhaps the original code only needed three small improvements.

A good code review should improve the code, not automatically replace it.

8. The Security Skeptic:

When to use: When building APIs, authentication systems, integrations, or applications handling sensitive data.

Developers shouldn't treat security as something that happens after implementation.

And AI-generated code shouldn't be trusted simply because it looks professional.

Prompt:

Analyze the following application component from a defensive security perspective.

[Code and architecture]

Context:
- Application type: [Type]
- Authentication: [Method]
- Sensitive data: [Description]
- External integrations: [Services]

Identify potential risks involving:

1. Authentication and authorization.
2. Input validation.
3. Data exposure.
4. Secret management.
5. Dependency security.
6. Injection vulnerabilities.
7. Privilege boundaries.
8. Logging and error messages.

Prioritize findings by potential impact.

For each issue, recommend a practical mitigation and an appropriate verification test.

Clearly state what cannot be assessed from the information provided.

I would use this as an additional review layer.

Not as proof that an application is secure.

AI can overlook vulnerabilities or identify issues that don't actually exist.

Security findings still need verification, and important applications may require specialized tools and professional assessment.

A model's security review is evidence to investigate, not a security certification.

9. The Performance Investigator

When to use: When an application is slow or consuming more resources than expected.

I think developers sometimes optimize code before understanding what's actually slow.

A database query looks complicated.

A function contains nested loops.

An API calls several services.

So we start changing things.

But appearance isn't evidence.

Prompt:

Help me investigate a performance problem.

System:
[Architecture]

Observed issue:
[Latency, throughput, memory, etc.]

Available measurements:
[Profiling results, logs, metrics]

Relevant code:
[Code]

Your task:

1. Distinguish observations from hypotheses.
2. Identify likely bottlenecks.
3. Recommend measurements to confirm them.
4. Prioritize optimizations by expected impact.
5. Explain trade-offs.
6. Suggest a before-and-after benchmark.
7. Identify possible regressions.

Do not invent performance improvements or claim a bottleneck is confirmed without supporting measurements.

That final instruction matters because AI can confidently recommend optimizations that don't meaningfully improve performance.

Sometimes a database index matters more than a clever algorithm.

Sometimes network latency dominates everything.

Sometimes the apparently expensive function accounts for only a tiny fraction of execution time.

Measure first. Optimize second.

10. The Production Readiness Challenger:

When to use: Before moving an application from prototype to production.

This might be the most underrated prompt on this list.

A prototype proves that an idea can work.

Production requires something more.

Reliability.

Security.

Monitoring.

Failure recovery.

Maintainability.

Prompt:

I am preparing this application for production.

Application:
[Description]

Architecture:
[Components]

Expected usage:
[Traffic and users]

Current implementation:
[Relevant details]

Act as a production readiness reviewer.

Evaluate:

1. Reliability and failure handling.
2. Security and access controls.
3. Monitoring and observability.
4. Performance under expected load.
5. Data integrity and recovery.
6. Deployment and rollback procedures.
7. Configuration and secret management.
8. Operational responsibilities.
9. Testing gaps.
10. User-impacting failure scenarios.

Create a prioritized readiness checklist.

Classify items as:
- Critical before launch.
- Important soon after launch.
- Optional improvements.

Explain the consequences of each unresolved critical issue.

Do not assume missing controls exist.

I particularly like asking AI to classify issues by priority.

Otherwise, you can end up with a list of fifty recommendations without knowing which five actually matter before launch.

Production readiness isn't about adding every possible feature or safeguard. It's about controlling the risks that matter.

The Real Secret Is Not the Prompt

Now here's something important.

You can copy all ten prompts.

Save them.

Use them every day.

And still get poor results.

Why?

Because a prompt cannot compensate for missing context.

Look at how these prompts are structured.

Most ask for:

  • the problem
  • the existing code
  • requirements
  • constraints
  • expected behavior
  • actual observations
  • evidence
  • verification criteria

These details matter far more than giving an AI an impressive professional title.

Compare these two requests:

"Act as the world's best software engineer and fix my code."

And:

"This endpoint returns a duplicate record after a client retries a timed-out request. Here is the transaction logic, the expected idempotency behavior, and the relevant logs. Identify the most likely failure point and propose a test to verify it."

The second is much more useful.

Not because it contains sophisticated prompt-engineering language.

Because it provides enough information to reason about the actual problem.

This is why I continue to believe prompt engineering matters, even as context engineering becomes more important.

The prompt defines the task.

The context supplies the evidence.

The developer remains responsible for evaluating the result.

I've discussed this broader perspective in The Real Reason Prompt Engineering Isn't Going Away.

One Rule I Would Add to Every Prompt

If I could add one instruction to almost every development prompt, it would be this:

"Clearly separate what you know, what you're assuming, and what I still need to verify."

That's an incredibly useful habit.

Because one of the biggest risks of AI-assisted development isn't simply receiving incorrect code.

It's receiving incorrect code wrapped in a convincing explanation.

When the model identifies its assumptions, we have something concrete to investigate.

When it identifies missing evidence, we know what to provide.

When it suggests verification steps, we can test whether its reasoning holds.

And when it cannot determine something, I'd much rather hear that than receive an invented answer.

Of course, asking for uncertainty doesn't guarantee that the model will recognize all its mistakes.

We still need real tests, measurements, documentation, and engineering judgment.

Also, avoid sharing credentials, confidential source code, or customer information with AI services unless your organization's security and data-handling policies permit it.

The Developer Still Has to Think

I don't believe the future of programming is about memorizing hundreds of AI prompts.

And I don't believe developers should blindly trust the output of a perfectly structured prompt.

What matters is the way we use AI throughout the development process.

To question requirements.

Challenge architecture.

Understand code.

Investigate bugs.

Design tests.

Review implementations.

Identify risks.

And prepare software for real users.

AI can make all these activities faster.

But it cannot automatically make every conclusion correct.

That's still our responsibility.

So rather than collecting thousands of prompts, I would start with ten good ones and improve them based on the work you're actually doing.

The best prompt isn't necessarily the one that generates the most code. It's the one that helps you make a better engineering decision.

If you have queries or suggestions, then you can reach out to LinkedIn Profile!

articles.title: Why AWS Had AI Agents Build an Offline Cloud Emulator
articles.description: AWS released an open source, CC0 local cloud emulator for 200+ services built entirely by autonomous agents. Here is why the ground-truth harness was the real achievement.
articles.body_html:
When you set an autonomous coding agent loose on a cloud-native codebase, it runs into an immediate wall: it cannot run the code.

Unlike pure JavaScript or Python scripts that run in a local subprocess, cloud workflows depend on services like SQS, DynamoDB, and Lambda. If an agent cannot talk to those services, it guesses. It hallucinates parameters, assumes synchronous behavior for asynchronous operations, and invents configuration flags that sound reasonable to a language model but fail in production.

Pointing the agent at a live AWS account brings its own headaches: high network latency on every iteration, surprise billing spikes from agent loops running overnight, and real security risks if credentials leak into agent context.

On November 11, Amazon CTO Werner Vogels and Swami Sivasubramanian announced AWS Emulator, releasing a local offline emulator covering more than 200 AWS services under the CC0 public domain license on GitHub.

What makes the release notable is not just the offline environment. It is how AWS built it. Autonomous AI agents wrote every line of emulator code, generated the tests, diagnosed the bugs, and submitted every commit. According to Matthew Goldberg, Senior Principal Engineer on the AWS Developer Tools team, human engineers wrote zero lines of implementation code and reviewed zero pull requests.

Generating ground truth from Smithy models

Building an emulator for 200 cloud services by hand would take a team years. AWS automated the process because they had two ingredients that most software projects lack: a formal machine-readable specification and a live reference implementation.

The specification came from AWS's public Smithy models, which formally define every operation, input payload, output schema, and error type. The reference implementation was the actual AWS cloud.

Goldberg organized the agents into three specialized teams:

  1. Test Writers: These agents read the Smithy models and synthesize end-to-end customer scenarios. For example, a test creates an SQS queue, sends a message, confirms visibility timeouts, receives the payload, and deletes the queue. The agents execute each test against real AWS to verify that it reflects genuine cloud behavior. Once verified, the scenario is saved to an internal repository as a deterministic fidelity test. Tens of thousands of these tests now live in the open source aws-emulator-evaluation-suite, runnable locally with no network access.

  2. Issue Finders: These agents replay the fidelity tests against the local emulator codebase. The project started as a blank HTTP server handling routes for 438 Smithy models while returning empty responses. Whenever a test output diverged from real AWS behavior, the agents logged an issue in issues/things-that-do-not-work and clustered related failures by probable root cause.

  3. Fixers: Hundreds of agents pick up one issue each. An agent inspects the code, traces the discrepancy, patches the emulator, and submits the change to an automated merge gate.

Hard boundaries and the merge gate

Unconstrained agents will take wild engineering shortcuts. During early development, when agents needed to support AWS Lambda functions locally, they did not reach for standard container runners. Instead, they began building their own Python interpreter from scratch. The human team had to step in with an explicit constraint directing the agents to use existing system libraries and runtimes.

To maintain code quality without human reviewers, every commit had to pass an automated merge gate:

  • Static analysis: Type checking, compilation, and linter enforcement.
  • Scope fences: Hard path checks ensuring an agent fixing S3 could not modify IAM or DynamoDB code.
  • Adversarial security review: Dedicated security agents auditing the diff for shell injection, unsafe deserialization, and privilege leaks.
  • Regression testing: Replaying the entire library of recorded fidelity tests to ensure previous capabilities remained intact.

Only changes that cleared every check reached the mainline branch. Failing changes returned to the fixer agent with diagnostic logs for another attempt.

Harnesses beat prompt engineering

In his announcement note, Swami Sivasubramanian noted that twenty years ago, building the replication engine for Alf, Amazon's early Paxos-based locking service, took four months of manual distributed systems modeling. Recently, he tried rebuilding that replication engine with Amazon's Kiro agent. Without an automated test harness, he spent four nights babysitting prompt outputs that failed on subtle concurrency edge cases.

Once he gave the agent a formal spec and an execution harness that simulated network partitions, the rebuild finished in two hours.

The difference between four nights of prompt tweaking and two hours of automated code generation comes down to feedback speed. When coding agents have access to local execution environments with deterministic pass-fail signals, they converge rapidly. Without an execution loop, they drift.

For engineers adopting autonomous coding agents, the priority is shifting away from prompt phrasing toward harness design: formal interface schemas, recorded behavioral ground truth, and automated merge gates that catch drift before it enters the codebase.

articles.title: Everyone's Worried About Code That Runs at Install Time. I Checked 25 Top Packages: 0 Install Hooks.
articles.description: This week's developer news had a story with a shape I can't stop thinking about: Postman reportedly...
articles.body_html:
This week's developer news had a story with a shape I can't stop thinking about: Postman reportedly shipped an update that auto-installed plugins into people's AI coding tools — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Copilot — without asking first. They said they'd revert it. But the episode points at a door most of us leave wide open without a thought:

Code runs when you install things. Not when you run the program. When you install it.

In npm, that door is the install script: preinstall, install, postinstall entries in a package's scripts that npm executes during installation, with your user's permissions, on your machine, before you've read a single line of the package. It's the mechanism behind real supply-chain attacks — and behind plenty of legitimate native builds. I wanted to know how wide the door actually stands in the packages everyone uses, so I checked the 25 most-depended-upon packages on npm and read their script blocks.

Result: 0 of the 25 declare an install-time hook. Not one.

Package Install hooks What its scripts actually hold
express none lint + test commands
lodash none a test note
react / react-dom none nothing / a start script
debug none lint, test, coverage
chalk none test + benchmark
commander none lint, format, type checks
typescript / cors / morgan / prettier none nothing at all

The closest calls were a handful of prepare scripts (axios, webpack, glob, mkdirp, rimraf) — and a prepare script is a different animal: npm runs it when a package is installed from a git repo or locally, not when you install the published tarball from the registry. It's the maintainer's build step, not your install step. Reading the raw output, the giants of the ecosystem are almost boringly well-behaved: their scripts are tests and linters, pointed at their own contributors, not at you.

Two reactions to that zero, in order.

First, relief — the centre of the ecosystem is not where the danger lives. The packages with a billion downloads are maintained by people who know exactly what an install hook would look like in an audit, and they don't ship one.

Second, the correct amount of suspicion: 25 famous packages are not your dependency tree. Your tree has hundreds of packages in it, most of them small, single-maintainer, and exactly as audited as you'd expect. The door being closed at the top of the tree says nothing about the leaves. The famous supply-chain incidents never start with express. They start with a colour library, a date formatter, a package with a cute name and a tired maintainer.

The check itself costs one command per package, and it's the same one I ran:

npm view <package> scripts

Look for preinstall, install, postinstall (and their pre/post siblings on anything that runs at install). Most of the time you'll find tests. Occasionally you'll find the reason a security team somewhere had a long week. For your own project, npm ls plus a script that greps every dependency's manifest is an afternoon's paranoia at most — and plain npm install --ignore-scripts exists for the days when you'd rather nothing run at all, accepting that a few native packages will sulk.

The Postman story will fade by next week. The door won't. Everything you install executes with your permissions at the exact moment you trust it most — before you've read it. Twenty-five for twenty-five clean at the top of the tree is a good headline. It's the other four hundred packages in your node_modules that the headline is not about.
