articles.title: The Question I Never Asked
articles.description: The word landed in the middle of a Tuesday meeting, in the big room, the one where the air...
articles.body_html:
The word landed in the middle of a Tuesday meeting, in the big room, the one where the air conditioner hummed like it was thinking about quitting.

We were redesigning the sync service, and the lead said, "We'll go with eventual consistency on this one," and kept talking like he had just said something normal, like "we'll use Postgres" or "let's order lunch." Everyone around the table made small agreeing noises. I made one too. Then I nodded.

I had a whole technique for the nod by then, though I didn't know it yet. It was slow, two beats, chin down and up, with a little pen tap at the end, as if the nod had a full stop. It said: yes, of course, eventual consistency, the obvious choice, carry on. It said all of that in half a second, and none of it was true. I had no idea what eventual consistency was. I had heard the words before, the way you hear a song on the radio and can hum the chorus but not name the band. Consistency. Eventually. Something about databases agreeing with each other, probably. Eventually.

The meeting moved on. I wrote the words in my notebook and put a star next to them, the way you star a message you plan to read later and never do.

Afterwards, back at my desk, I googled it: "eventual consistency simple explanation." The first result was a blog post with a diagram of two databases holding hands. The second was a Wikipedia page that used the word "convergence" in the first sentence and lost me by the third. The third was a forum answer that began, "Actually, it's quite simple," and then ran for nine hundred words. I read all three. I closed all three. I understood it the way you understand a joke someone explains to you: the words went in, the meaning waved at me from a distance and kept walking.

So I did what I always did. I nodded harder.

That is the part nobody tells you about the nod. It works. That is the problem. Nobody checks. Meetings move fast, and a confident nod is a tiny green light. The lead saw mine and kept going. The next week, someone said "idempotency" and I nodded at that too, and wrote it in the notebook with another star. The week after that it was "backpressure." By March the notebook had eleven stars. Eleven words I had nodded at and never looked up. My notebook started to look like a star chart. I told myself I would look them all up on Friday. I never looked them up on Friday. Friday was for the things I had already put off on Thursday.

I started rehearsing explanations in the shower. That was the lowest point, probably, though I didn't know it then. I would stand there with the water going cold and explain eventual consistency to the tiles, in a confident voice, using words like "convergence" that I had stolen from the Wikipedia page. The tiles were a generous audience. They never asked follow-up questions.

The dread came later, and it came in a specific shape. It was not the fear of being found out in general. It was the fear of one sentence: "Salam, what do you think?" The lead said it the way leads do, casually, eyes scanning the room for someone who had been quiet. I had been quiet because I was busy nodding. I started volunteering to take the meeting notes, because a man writing things down has a reason to look at his notebook instead of at the lead. My notes were excellent. My notes were the best notes in the team. They were also a hiding place with bullet points.

Once, I nearly asked. The lead said "backpressure" and I actually opened my mouth, and then a senior engineer asked a question about the queue depth, a real question with numbers in it, and the moment closed like a door. I told myself the timing was wrong. The timing was always wrong.

The worst part was that I was not stupid. I knew that, in the way you know things at 2 a.m. and forget by 10. I could build the thing. I could read the code. I just could not say the words out loud without feeling like someone would ask me to keep going, and then I would be standing there with an empty bucket and a long way to the well. So I kept the bucket hidden and nodded.

Then, one Thursday, the bucket came out anyway.

It was a sprint review. The product manager asked whether users would see their updates straight away, and I heard myself say, "It's eventually consistent, so, you know, a few seconds, max." I said it the way I had heard other people say it: lightly, confidently, like a man describing his own kitchen. And then Maya, the senior dev, who was refilling her water bottle by the window, said, "Eventually doesn't have a max. That's the whole deal. It could be a second. It could be an hour, if something's stuck. Eventually is a promise without a deadline."

She said it the way you tell someone the lift is out of order. No smile of victory, no pause for the room to enjoy it. She just said it, and sat down, and the meeting went on. Nobody laughed. Nobody even looked at me the way I had spent a year imagining people would look at me. The product manager said "ah, okay, good to know," and wrote something down. The floor did not open. The sky did not fall. I sat there with my face burning and a strange feeling underneath the burning, like the moment after you take a plaster off and find the skin underneath is fine.

That evening I looked it up properly. Not the frantic googling of before. I read one article slowly, with the notebook open, and I wrote down what it meant in my own words, the way you would explain it to a friend: the system promises the copies will agree, but it does not promise when. I wrote that sentence twice. Then I looked up idempotency, and backpressure, and three other stars. It took forty minutes. Forty minutes, for a year of dread. I did the maths on that and decided not to do the maths on that. Then I closed the laptop and went for a walk, and I felt something I had not felt in a year of meetings. I felt like I had put down a bag I had forgotten I was carrying.

The next week, the lead said "idempotency" again. I heard myself say, "Sorry — quick one. When you say idempotent, you mean we can run the same request twice and nothing bad happens, right?"

The room did something I did not expect. Two people visibly relaxed, the way people relax when someone else says the thing they were thinking. One of them laughed and said, "Thank god. I was going to google that tonight." And Maya, from her corner, said, "I have a bookmark folder for this stuff. I look it up every single time. Eleven years in, and I still check."

Eleven years. She had been doing this eleven years, and she still checked. I thought about my notebook full of stars. I thought about the hiding place with bullet points. I almost laughed, right there in the meeting, and I had to turn it into a cough.

After that, the questions got easier, the way anything gets easier once you have done it once and survived. I asked about backpressure. I asked about the retry policy. Once I asked a question and the answer was something I actually knew, and I felt foolish for about four seconds, and then I forgot about it, because nobody else remembered it either. I asked a question in a meeting with the client, and the client said, "Good question, I was wondering that too," and I wrote that down in the notebook as well, without a star, because some things you do not need to look up later.

A year later, almost to the week, I was in the same big room, the same air conditioner still thinking about quitting, and the lead said "eventual consistency" again. This time I was the one who had been in the room the longest. And across the table, a new engineer, first week, did the nod. The slow nod. Two beats. Chin down and up. And then the pen tap, the little full stop. I knew that nod the way you know your own handwriting. I still have the notebook. The stars are still there.

After the meeting I caught him by the kettle. "Hey," I said. "Eventual consistency. It just means the copies promise to agree, but nobody promises when. That's all it is."

He looked at me, and his shoulders did something I recognised. They went down, half an inch, like he had put down a bag.

"Oh," he said. "That's it?"

"That's it," I said.

He nodded. And so did I. This time I knew what I was nodding at.

articles.title: I Built a 17-Year-Old Tetris Game With Today's GCC. It Threw 27 Errors First.
articles.description: $ make build util.c frame.c shapes.c tetris.c CC -Wall util.c frame.c shapes.c tetris.c /usr/bin/ld:...
articles.body_html:
$ make
build util.c frame.c shapes.c tetris.c
CC -Wall util.c frame.c shapes.c tetris.c
/usr/bin/ld: /tmp/ccMMTOCD.o:(.bss+0x0): multiple definition of `tv'; /tmp/ccTozTNs.o:(.bss+0x0): first defined here
/usr/bin/ld: /tmp/ccMMTOCD.o:(.bss+0x80): multiple definition of `frame'; /tmp/ccTozTNs.o:(.bss+0x80): first defined here
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
make: *** [Makefile:16: tty-tetris] Error 1

That was the first thing the program ever said to me. No binary, no game, just the linker refusing to do its job. Twenty-seven errors, and the code had not run a single line yet.

This week dev.to is full of people waking up dead code, so I picked a patient of my own: a Tetris clone called tty-tetris, sitting untouched on GitHub since 15 January 2009. Ten commits in its whole life, the first one on Christmas Day 2008. Seventeen years and ten months of silence. I wanted to know what happens when you take code that old and feed it to a compiler from 2026 without changing a thing.

The patient

The repo is xorg62/tty-tetris, described by its author as "a simple tetris game wrote in C (without ncurses)". I picked it for three reasons, and all three are boring on purpose. It is small: 786 lines of C and headers across four .c files, plus a 37-line Makefile. It has zero outside dependencies, no ncurses, no X11, just termios and ANSI escape codes, so nothing else had to be installed or hunted down. And it was genuinely abandoned, not just quiet for a year: the last commit message reads "Modify nextbox", and then nothing, ever.

The Makefile is seven lines of real content. It compiles four files with cc -Wall and calls the result tty-tetris. My machine runs GCC 13.3.0 and GNU Make 4.3, both stock Ubuntu. Nothing exotic. That was the whole setup, and it still fell over.

What 27 errors actually means

The error count sounds dramatic, but it is really one mistake repeated. Nine global variables live in the shared header tetris.h:

const int shapes[7][4][4][2];
struct itimerval tv;
struct termios back_attr;
shape_t current;
int frame[FRAMEH + 1][FRAMEW + 1];
int frame_nextbox[FRAMEH_NB][FRAMEW_NB];
int score;
int lines;
Bool running;

Every one of the four .c files includes that header. So the compiler builds four copies of each variable, one per file, and hands all four to the linker. The linker sees score defined four times and says no. Nine variables times three extra copies each gives you the 27 "multiple definition" lines in my build log, plus one fatal ld returned 1 exit status at the end.

Here is the part that makes this a story about time rather than a bug. This code was never correct by the letter of the C standard. It was tolerated. GCC before version 10 defaulted to -fcommon, a mode that quietly merges duplicate tentative definitions into one, the way a tired teacher might let a repeated answer slide. GCC 10 flipped the default to -fno-common. The rule did not change. The enforcement did. Code written in 2008 compiled fine for a decade on a compiler that was being polite, and then the politeness ended.

That is the real shape of "legacy code" in my experience now. The bits do not decay. Nothing in those 786 lines changed since 2009. The ground moved under them instead: stricter defaults, removed functions, headers that moved. The program is frozen. The world is not.

The fix: one line

I had two ways to fix this. The proper one is to rewrite the header so the variables are declared extern there and defined exactly once in a single .c file. That is the right repair, and it touches nine lines across two files. The minimal one is to tell the compiler to be polite again. I took the minimal one, because the point of the exercise was resurrection, not renovation:

-CFLAGS = -Wall
+CFLAGS = -Wall -fcommon

One flag in the Makefile. No source file touched. I rebuilt, and the whole tone of the output changed:

build util.c frame.c shapes.c tetris.c
CC -Wall -fcommon util.c frame.c shapes.c tetris.c

Make exited 0. Errors: 0. The binary landed at 21,808 bytes, an ELF 64-bit executable, built from code older than some of the laptops it now runs on.

Eight warnings survived the fix, and I left them alone on purpose. All eight are the same warning, twice per source file: variably modified 'frame' at file scope, pointing at tetris.h:112. The frame dimensions are defined as (int)(9*2.3) and (int)(10*2.3), casts of floating-point math, which C does not accept as a true constant for a file-scope array size. The compiler grumbles and carries on. It is a warning, not an error, and fixing it would mean editing the original author's arithmetic. I wanted the game, not a rewrite, so the warnings stay as a small plaque on the wall: this code is old, it knows it, and it still works.

The run

A Tetris game needs a terminal, so I opened one, played a few moves, hit rotate once, and then q to quit. It drew its frame, showed Score: and Lines: 0, redrew as the pieces fell, and when I pressed q it said goodbye in the most 2009 way possible:

Bye! Your score: 0

Exit code 0. Three seconds of play, a game I lost on purpose. The score was 0 because I quit before clearing a line, not because the game was broken. It played. The pieces fell, the frame held, the quit key worked exactly as config.h promised back in 2008.

So the final tally: 27 errors, 8 warnings, 1 changed line, 0 changed source files, 1 working game, and a score of 0 that I earned honestly.

What I actually learned

The tempting lesson is "old code is fragile", but the run says the opposite. The code was fine. It did exactly what it did in 2009, the moment I gave it a compiler willing to accept its one bad habit. What changed was the contract between the code and the tools, and that contract changes silently, one default flag at a time, while nobody is watching the repo.

That matters more than it sounds, because most abandoned code dies this way: not from a bug anyone found, but from a toolchain that stopped forgiving it. The fix here cost one flag and ten minutes, most of which was reading the linker output properly instead of panicking at the count. The 27 errors were one error wearing 27 coats.

If you have a dead program of your own sitting in a repo somewhere, try this before you rewrite it. Clone it, run the build, and read the first error all the way to the end. Count how many of the errors are the same one. You might find the patient was never dead at all. It was just waiting for someone to argue with the linker on its behalf.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: My Cron Job Fired 50 Times While the Receiver Was Down. 10 Webhooks Vanished.
articles.description: Fifty POSTs, one per second, each carrying its own idempotency key. At fire 21, I killed the...
articles.body_html:
Fifty POSTs, one per second, each carrying its own idempotency key. At fire 21, I killed the receiver.

That was the whole experiment. A dispatcher on my laptop, a receiver on the same laptop, and a kill signal in the middle. I wanted a number, not an opinion: when the thing on the other end dies mid-run, how much of a cron job's work actually arrives?

The dispatcher is a small Node script. It fires 50 POSTs to localhost, one a second, keys evt-001 through evt-050. Every POST carries an Idempotency-Key header with its key. If an attempt fails, it waits 500 milliseconds and tries once more, then moves on. It never asks why anything failed. It fires, it logs, it moves on.

The receiver is even smaller. It takes each POST, writes one JSON line to a log file, and answers 200. In phase 1 it ignores the idempotency key completely. It has no memory, no database, no queue. It is the dumbest possible webhook endpoint, which is the point. Most receivers I have actually built were not much smarter than this.

A controller script ran the outage. It watched the dispatcher log, killed the receiver after fire 21's ACK landed, and started it again after fire 31's retry failed. The outage is defined by delivery count, not by the clock, so exactly ten deliveries fell inside it: fires 22 through 31. No stopwatch, no guessing.

Phase 1, the dispatcher log for the first lost key:

{"ts":"2026-11-11T21:06:01.251Z","key":"evt-022","n":22,"attempt":1,"result":"error","error":"ECONNREFUSED"}

Ten keys, evt-022 to evt-031, each with two error lines: the first attempt, then the retry 500 ms later, also refused. Twenty error lines in total. Everything else got an ACK.

The receiver log, when the run finished: 40 lines, all "delivered", zero duplicates. First line evt-001, last line evt-050, with a hole in the middle where the outage was.

So the count is 40 delivered, 10 lost, 0 duplicated. The title of this post is the result, not a guess. Ten webhooks vanished, and nothing I had built noticed. The dispatcher logged the errors and carried on. The receiver had nothing to log because it was dead. If this had been a real cron job syncing orders or sending receipts, ten of them would simply not exist, and the only trace would be error lines in a log file nobody reads at 3 a.m.

The retry deserves a closer look, because it feels like it should have saved something. It saved nothing. The retry fires 500 ms after the failure, and the outage lasted about fifteen seconds of dispatcher time. A retry only helps when the outage is shorter than the retry delay. Mine was thirty times longer. A retry is a seatbelt for a stumble, not a parachute for a fall. I wrote it in because every tutorial says to add a retry, and it did exactly nothing for the failure I actually had.

Phase 2. Same fifty fires, same ten-delivery outage. Two changes: the receiver now honours the idempotency key, and after the run I replay the keys that never got an ACK.

First, the honest part. The header alone recovers nothing. I want to be plain about that, because the draft description I wrote before running this said "then added one header and ran it again", as if the header were the fix. It is not the fix. The header is a promise the receiver has to keep. Phase 2 before the replay looked exactly like phase 1: 40 delivered, the same ten keys lost, zero duplicates. The header changed nothing while the receiver was dead, because a dead receiver keeps no promises.

What changed the numbers was the replay. After the dispatcher finished, a second script read its log, picked out the ten keys with no ACK, and sent each one again. All ten came back {"status":"ok"}. Ten recovered, zero still lost.

Then I ran the replay a second time, with all fifty keys, to see what the header actually buys. Every single one came back {"status":"duplicate"}. Fifty out of fifty recognised, zero re-processed. The receiver log ended at 100 lines: 50 delivered, 50 duplicate entries, 50 unique keys. Every key delivered exactly once.

That is the whole story. The replay recovers the lost work, and the idempotency key makes the replay safe. Without the key, replaying all fifty would have delivered forty of them twice. With the key, the second pass is a no-op. The pieces only work together. A retry without a replay recovers nothing. A replay without an idempotency key doubles your deliveries. The header without either is decoration.

There are limits, and I should name them, because this ran on one laptop. Localhost has no real network latency, no half-delivered POSTs, no receiver that writes the log line and dies before answering. In production the failure modes are uglier: a POST can land and its response can still be lost, which is the one case where a retry does create a duplicate, and it is the case my setup could not produce. The numbers here are for this setup. They are not a promise about a queue in production.

What I would actually build, after watching this run, is boring. The dispatcher keeps an outbox: every event written down before it is sent, with its key. A sweeper re-sends anything with no ACK, on a timer, until it gets one. The receiver keeps every key it has seen in a real store, not a log file, and answers "duplicate" for repeats. That is three small pieces, and none of them is clever. The clever version is the one I started with: fire and forget, one quick retry, hope the other end stays up. It lost ten out of fifty.

Twenty-six posts in the last seven days on dev.to argued about cron webhook recovery patterns, and twenty-five more about rate-limited queues and dead-letter recovery. Most of them debate retry counts and backoff curves. After counting my own losses, I think the debate is pointed at the wrong piece. The retry count barely mattered. The replay sweep and the key were the whole game.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: Local AI models need to be a browser feature
articles.description: I started thinking about the Web Models API while experimenting with building AI-native GUIs. I was...
articles.body_html:
I started thinking about the Web Models API while experimenting with building AI-native GUIs. I was exploring the idea of UI as a function of AI: the model would generate the content and choose the component best suited to display it.

One experiment was a news site which used LLMs to identify key topics (people, places, or things) in an article and turn those topics into links. A reader could click on a topic to get more context, presented in a component suited to that content.

While working on demos I kept running into the same problem. Running an LLM in the browser with WebAssembly or WebGPU meant having the app load and run the model itself, and the performance wasn't good enough for what I was building. Using a cloud provider meant paying for usage, even when I just wanted to share a demo.

That got me thinking about what this means for indie developers. Putting an experiment or small product online can mean an ongoing bill before you know whether anyone finds it useful or have a way to fund it.

I wanted web apps to use on-device models with the user's permission, much like asking to use a camera or microphone. This led me to build my first attempt at solving this. Browser.AI was a prototype that exposed an API on the window object to access models running on-device. The learnings from that became the foundation for the Web Models API proposal.

Web Models API — Models belong in every browser.

A proposed browser API for web apps that need a particular open-weight model. People control access; the browser runs it. Join the Web Models API discussion.

webmodels.dev

How it works

The Web Models API exposes access to open-weight on-device models through a simple verb oriented API on navigator.models. The app requests an open-weight model using a universal ID so developers can target the exact model release they built and tested against.

The user decides if a site can access that model, and at any point can revoke access. The permission is tied to the model and site pairing, so permission to use one model does not give the site access to every model on the device.

The browser sets up and runs models, manages resource use, and shares model weights across sites. Each app doesn't need their own copy of the model, but the data and permissions stay separate.

The API also supports tool calls, structured output, and multimedia. An app could provide functions for filtering a list, choosing a component, or updating a form; the model requests a function call, and the app checks it before running it. Structured output means the app gets back JSON it can render directly, not text it has to parse. Multimedia input means a model can take an image directly, useful for something like a receipt reader.

So for my news site experiment, the app would still decide what context to send, check the model's response, and render the selected component. The browser handles running the model.

Cost and control

When a suitable model can run on the user's device, you don't need a paid cloud inference service. For me, this is also about control: over where our money goes, and over where our users' data goes. Developers should be able to decide when paying a cloud provider adds value and when a local model is enough.

In many cases there's no good reason to send that data to a server when the same task can run securely on the user's machine. Someone filling out a tax form or discussing a medical scan shouldn't have to trust that data to a cloud provider when the device they're using can do the job.

There are also reasons to run locally beyond cost and privacy. A notes app could search personal documents without sending their contents to a model provider, and with the model, app, and documents available locally, that search works offline. Local processing also skips the network round trip.

Why model choice matters

I believe competitive open-weight models are an important part of that future. Different tasks need different models. A small model may be enough to choose a UI component. Document search needs an embedding model. A receipt reader needs a model that can handle images. Developers should be able to choose based on what works for their app, independently of which browser someone uses.
The Prompt API provides access to a browser specified language model. But apps often end up tuning their prompts to one model's quirks. Those prompts may work poorly in another browser or after a model update.

In my UI experiments, the model's ability to identify content and select the right component was part of how the app worked. A different model could make different choices. You'll run into the same issue if you want to use embeddings for document search: an app must use the same embedding model to index documents and later search them. Developers need a defined model target they can test, and a way to choose when to move to a new release.

Being forced to use the model a big tech company shipped with their browser makes us developers dependent on their internal business strategies. For example, if they decide that on-device inference is a challenge to their cloud business, they might be less motivated to improve the model. I want developers and users to have real alternatives, with less dependence on a few companies' pricing, model choices, and decisions about how their services work.

Help shape it

I care about this because I want to keep building and sharing useful and interesting applications of AI, and I want other developers to be able to do the same. Funding an expensive cloud inference bill and sending your users' data into a black box shouldn't be requirements to access AI, especially when the task can run on hardware the user already has.

The Web Models API is still early, and I'd like to hear from developers.

If you could run a specific open-weight model in any browser, for free, what would you build? Which model would you use? If you've already shipped AI features with Transformers.js, the Prompt API, or a cloud provider, what got in your way?

Let me know in the comments. The explainer and API reference are on Github if you want the details. In the next post, I'll walk through the API with code.

articles.title: What it takes to prove binary search works
articles.description: I used Dafny to verify binary search, broke its termination, and compiled the working version to JavaScript.
articles.body_html:
In my previous article about Proof Driven Development, I wrote about using formal specifications to check whether code does what we agreed it should do. Microsoft Research's PDD Kit uses Verus for Rust, though, and most of my work is in JavaScript. So I was left with a question: what can I actually try without rewriting my whole application in Rust?

I ended up trying Dafny. With help from a coding agent, I wrote and verified a small binary search, deliberately broke it, and compiled the working version to JavaScript.

If you haven't heard of Dafny, it's an open-source programming language and verifier. You write code and describe what must be true before and after it runs. Dafny checks the code against those rules using a solver called Z3, and can compile it to languages including JavaScript.

dafny-lang / dafny

Dafny is a verification-aware programming language

Dafny

Dafny is a verification-ready programming language. As you type in your program, Dafny's verifier constantly looks over your shoulder, flags any errors, shows you counterexamples, and congratulates you when your code matches your specifications. When you're done, Dafny can compile your code to C#, Go, Python, Java, or JavaScript (more to come!), so it can integrate with your existing workflow.

Dafny will give you assurance that your code meets the specifications you write, while letting you write both code and specifications in the Dafny programming language itself. Since verification is an integral part of development, it will thus reduce the risk of costly late-stage bugs that are typically missed by testing.

Dafny has support for common programming concepts such as classes and trait inheritance, inductive datatypes that can have methods and are suitable for pattern matching, lazily unbounded datatypes, subset types e.g. for bounded integers…

View on GitHub

What is Z3?

Z3 is a solver: you give it logical constraints and it checks whether they can be satisfied. Dafny uses it to help check whether the code could violate the rules we wrote.

Why binary search?

If you don't know binary search, don't worry: the internet definitely doesn't have enough articles about it yet. I even wrote one of them a few years ago, including the most important requirement:

  • Your list must be sorted.
  • Your list must be sorted.
  • Your list must be sorted.

Still true! Binary search looks at the middle of a sorted collection, discards the half that can't contain the value, and repeats. That sounds simple until you have to decide what happens with an empty array, a missing value, duplicates, or a search range with one element left.

I wanted to see what it would take to check those cases without listing each input in a test. So I wrote down what a correct result should look like and asked Dafny to check the implementation against it.

What are we actually promising?

Here's the contract I used:

method BinarySearch(a: array<int>, key: int) returns (index: int)
  requires forall i, j ::
    0 <= i < j < a.Length ==> a[i] <= a[j]

  ensures index == -1 <==>
    forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] != key

  ensures index != -1 ==>
    0 <= index < a.Length && a[index] == key

requires is the condition the caller must satisfy: the array is sorted in ascending order. Equal values are allowed.

The first ensures says the result is -1 if and only if the value is absent. The second says that any other result must be a valid index containing the value. If there are duplicates, returning any matching index is fine; this contract doesn't ask for the first one.

In other words, there are two cases: if the value is missing, return -1; if it exists, return an index where it appears. Both clauses work together: the first describes when -1 is allowed, and the second checks that any other result points to the value.

The implementation needs an explanation too

Here is the complete method, including the loop invariants:

method BinarySearch(a: array<int>, key: int) returns (index: int)
  requires forall i, j ::
    0 <= i < j < a.Length ==> a[i] <= a[j]
  ensures index == -1 <==>
    forall k :: 0 <= k < a.Length ==> a[k] != key
  ensures index != -1 ==>
    0 <= index < a.Length && a[index] == key
{
  var low := 0;
  var high := a.Length;

  while low < high
    invariant 0 <= low <= high <= a.Length
    invariant forall k :: 0 <= k < low ==> a[k] < key
    invariant forall k :: high <= k < a.Length ==> key < a[k]
    decreases high - low
  {
    var mid := low + (high - low) / 2;

    if a[mid] < key {
      low := mid + 1;
    } else if key < a[mid] {
      high := mid;
    } else {
      return mid;
    }
  }

  return -1;
}

The search range is [low, high): it includes low, but not high. At the beginning, that's the whole array. At the end, when low == high, there's nothing left to search.

The invariants describe what must remain true throughout the loop. The first keeps the range inside the array. The other two say that everything before low is smaller than the key, and everything at or after high is larger. If we find the key, we return its index. If the range becomes empty, those two facts explain why the key can't be anywhere in the array.

decreases high - low is the termination argument. The verifier checks that the remaining range gets smaller on each iteration that continues the loop. Without that check, we could miss a search that gets stuck repeating the same step.

With Dafny 4.11.0, the verifier reported:

Dafny program verifier finished with 3 verified, 0 errors

Those three verified items are the verifier's reported count for the sample; they aren't a count of all the individual properties. The method's contract, bounds and termination are checked under its precondition. Dafny's guide goes into more detail on preconditions, postconditions and invariants.

Getting Started with Dafny: A Guide | Dafny Documentation

dafny.org

Let's break it

I changed one line:

- low := mid + 1;
+ low := mid;

The middle value is too small, so moving the lower bound to the middle might seem reasonable. But we already checked that position; we need to move past it.

Suppose we're looking for 6 and only 5 remains. low and mid are both 2, so setting low to mid leaves the range exactly where it was:

The next iteration checks 5 again, and the one after that does the same. With low := mid + 1, low becomes 3, the range is empty, and the search returns -1.

Dafny rejected the changed version:

Error: decreases expression might not decrease

Dafny program verifier finished with 2 verified, 1 error

The error doesn't spell out the one-element case, but it points us to the right place: the search range isn't guaranteed to shrink.

But I write JavaScript

Dafny can compile to JavaScript. I compiled this sample with dafny build --target js and ran the generated program with Node. For [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], it returned 3 for 7 and -1 for 4.

Installation Instructions | Dafny Documentation

dafny.org

The generated JavaScript uses bignumber.js for Dafny integers. It also includes generated runtime code, so this isn't the same experience as adding a type annotation to an existing JavaScript function. To call the generated method from an application, we need an integration layer that supplies values in the expected representation. I tried that separately with a small session-policy function; the generated sample needed an export added before a Node wrapper could call it.

And remember the first rule? The array must be sorted. Dafny checks that calls from verified Dafny code satisfy the requires clause; our sample's Main does. But the search method itself assumes its input is sorted, and the generated JavaScript doesn't automatically check an array supplied by a JavaScript caller. We need to establish that guarantee at the boundary or elsewhere in the application. Checking every element on every call takes linear time, which can outweigh the benefit of binary search.

We also need to check how the JavaScript adapter converts values. Dafny integers are mathematical integers; JavaScript Number values have their own limits.

The proof also doesn't establish that we picked the right behavior. If the product needs the first occurrence of a duplicate, our current contract allows a different matching index. Dafny can verify exactly what we asked for and still leave the product team asking why the result isn't the one they expected.

How is this different from TDD?

With TDD, I could start with a failing test for searching [5] for 6, then write the search until that test passes. That case would expose the broken low := mid update, although the test runner would need a timeout because the function gets stuck. I'd also add tests for an empty array, a value at either end, a missing value and duplicates.

Those tests check the inputs I chose. Dafny checks the method against the contract for all sorted integer arrays in its model, including the cases I didn't think to write down. It also checks that the loop makes progress, so I don't have to wait for a particular test to hang before finding that problem.

There's a tradeoff: I had to write the contract and loop invariants. If I forget to specify that the result should be the first matching index, Dafny won't invent that requirement for me. A test can miss the same requirement, but it's often easier to write and read a concrete example of what a user expects.

I'd still use tests around the generated JavaScript: they can check the adapter and real inputs from the application, which sit outside this proof. TDD would help me develop those behaviors one example at a time; Dafny gives me a way to check a general rule about the search itself.

What changes with AI?

Formal verification isn't new. What's changing for me is how practical it feels to try it. Learning a verification language, writing the specification and working out the loop invariants all take time. On top of building the feature, that can make verification a difficult sell.

Here, a coding agent helped write the Dafny example and work through the verification. That gave me something concrete to read and experiment with instead of starting from a blank file. I could change mid + 1 to mid, run the verifier again and see what happened. Getting to that point took less effort than learning the whole tool before trying a small example.

That doesn't mean I can accept whatever the agent writes. I still need to understand the contract well enough to notice that it allows any matching index, and check what happens when the code is called from JavaScript. But if AI can help with the mechanics and make these experiments cheaper, formal verification becomes something more of us can try on code where it would previously have been hard to justify the time.

articles.title: A black box is not redaction — and three other things I got wrong building local PDF tools
articles.description: Take any PDF. Draw a black rectangle over a line of text in a viewer that lets you annotate. Save it....
articles.body_html:
Take any PDF. Draw a black rectangle over a line of text in a viewer that lets you annotate. Save it. Open it again and drag-select across the rectangle.

The text comes back.

That is the entire reason I built a PDF tool site, and it is also the first thing I got wrong.

A black box is a drawing, not a deletion

An annotation is an object layered on top of the page content. The characters underneath are still there, in the content stream, encoded exactly as they were before you covered them up. Select-all still finds them. Copy still copies them. Any text extractor still returns them.

Actual redaction means the characters stop existing in the file. Not hidden, not covered, not rendered white-on-white — gone from the content stream, so that extraction returns nothing.

I built the redaction tool around that distinction, and then I made the checker report a number instead of a picture. Counting characters inside the marked areas turns out to be the only way to tell a real deletion from a good-looking one.

Three different zeros

This is the part that took me longest to get right, and it is the part most redaction tools skip.

If the checker says "0 characters inside the marked areas," that sentence can mean three completely different things:

  1. The text is gone. The page had a text layer, you marked it, and now extraction returns 0. This is the result you want, and the report calls it CLEARED.
  2. There was never a text layer. The page is a scan. Every pixel is an image; there are no characters to find in the first place. The tool reports NOTHING TO MEASURE, because the 0 is the absence of a measurement, not a clean result. A scanner output can look identical to a properly redacted page and mean the opposite thing — one has no text because it never did, the other has no text because you removed it.
  3. You drew the box on empty space. Same 0, same false comfort. The text you meant to remove is three lines down.

The first version of my checker merged all three into a single "0" with a green tick. That is a security product telling you what you want to hear. The current version reports the source page's character count next to the output's, so a scan and a clean redaction can never look the same.

There is a fourth result, and it is the ugly one: the marked page still hands back extractable text after processing. The report says so in plain words and tells you to treat the output like the original. It has happened in testing. I would rather the tool say that than round up to success.

What actually happens to the file

The redaction runs locally: the page is rendered to a canvas at 2× (about 144 DPI), the marked pages are rebuilt as JPEGs at quality 0.9, and the result is assembled into a new PDF. Pages you did not mark are copied through with their original text layer intact.

That has a consequence the tool states on the report rather than hides: a rebuilt page is an image, so everything on it stops being selectable — including the text that was not inside a box. If you need the rest of the page to stay searchable, you cannot have that and a destroyed text layer on the same page. Pick which one matters for this document.

The leak nobody looks at

Redaction is about what is visible. Metadata is about what is attached.

I stripped Title, Author, Subject and friends, and the file still carried the old title. The cause: pdf-lib removes the catalog's reference to the XMP packet, but the packet itself survives as an unreferenced indirect object inside the document. Delete the pointer and the body stays.

The second mistake was the check. I searched the output bytes for x:xmpmeta and found nothing, so I called it clean. The object was compressed. A byte search over a deflated stream tells you nothing at all — and this is exactly the kind of false pass that makes a verification step worse than no verification step.

The fix was to enumerate every indirect object after stripping, decompress each stream (UTF-8 first, then deflate, then raw deflate), and count the ones that still contain an XMP packet. Streams over 5 MB are reported as unscanned rather than silently skipped, because "I did not check this" and "this is clean" are different answers.

On my test file: 1,634 bytes in, 766 out, no XMP left. Compressed variant: 1,256 to 754.

Two more surprises, both about what tools quietly drop

Rebuilding a PDF is a destructive operation and the destructive part is not always where you expect.

PDFDocument.create() plus copyPages does not carry Author, Title or XMP into the new document — so a merge tool built this way produces a file with the contents of both inputs and the metadata of neither. It also stamps its own Producer and Creator as pdf-lib (...). If you were merging to preserve a document's provenance, you did not.

Same for splitting: each part is a fresh document, so each part arrives with no author and no title, whatever the original had. A tool page claiming otherwise is a page contradicting its own code.

The page-level limits are equally unglamorous: splitting one page per file caps at 50 pages, converting to JPG caps at 100, redaction caps at 50, and every tool caps the upload at 100 MB. These are browser limits, not policy — past that point memory pressure starts killing tabs, and a tool that crashes halfway is worse than one that refuses up front.

How to check that nothing is uploaded

This is the claim everything else rests on, so it should be falsifiable in ten seconds rather than taken on trust.

Open the tool, open the browser's Network tab, and drop a file in. You will see no request carrying your document. What you will see is static assets, and Cloudflare's analytics beacon, which the host injects into every page it serves — that is the CDN counting visits, not your file going anywhere. Clear the log, process the file, and watch it stay empty.

Five tools, all of them local

Everything above is implemented in the browser with pdf-lib and pdf.js. No server, no queue, no upload step, because there is nothing to upload to.

  • Redact a PDF without uploading it — draw boxes, rebuild the marked pages as images, get a report that separates the three zeros. Not a certification, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a compliance workflow that requires one.
  • Strip metadata from a PDF — Info dictionary and XMP, verified by decompressing every object rather than trusting the pointer deletion.
  • Merge PDFs in the browser — page contents carried, metadata deliberately not.
  • Split a PDF into single pages — one file per page or fixed ranges, zero-padded names so part10 sorts after part9 and not before part2.
  • Convert PDF pages to JPG — 144 or 216 DPI, quality 0.92 fixed, one download per page or a single ZIP.

Disclosure: these are my own tools. No affiliate links, nothing paid, no account required.

If you need redaction that survives opposing counsel, this is not that product, and I would rather say so here than in a support email. What it is: a local check you can run before you send a file you are not sure about.

articles.title: One day, nine updates: making a Bitcoin wallet in Kisumu reliable
articles.description: I build Ye₿ente, an open-source Bitcoin Lightning wallet, here in Kisumu, Kenya. It runs on my own...
articles.body_html:
I build Ye₿ente, an open-source Bitcoin Lightning wallet, here in Kisumu, Kenya. It runs on my own Lightning node, and it can pay any shop in kTown, a small network of local shops that take bitcoin and get paid in M-Pesa.

Today's work was about one thing: when someone taps Send, the money should actually go. Nine pull requests later, here is what changed and what I learned.

1. Sends were refused while the node was healthy

Users saw "Sending is paused while the wallet reconnects." The node was fine: synced, one active channel. So why?

Before every send, the server asks the node how much it can send. That read used the pay key, and the pay key could pay but couldn't read channel balances. The answer came back blank, and a blank meant "node unreachable", so every send was refused.

The fix: reads fall back to the node's read-only key. Neither key can move money through these calls.

// Reads about sending (channels, payments): the pay key first,
// then the read-only key.
async function readForPay(path, opts = {}) {
  const keys = [...new Set([process.env.YEBENTE_LND_PAY_MACAROON, READ()].filter(Boolean))];
  let last = new Error("No node key can read this.");
  for (const macaroon of keys) {
    try { return await lndRequest("GET", path, null, { ...opts, macaroon }); }
    catch (e) { last = e; }
  }
  throw last;
}

The new test fails on the old code with the exact error users saw, and passes with the fix. A security review checked the change before merge. (PR #495)

Lesson: least privilege is right, but test the reads your code depends on with the exact key it will use in production.

2. Never show "sent" for a payment that didn't go

When the node didn't answer in time, the server replied "pending", and the app still played the sent animation. Now a pending payment shows "Not confirmed yet", no celebration, and if it fails the sats come back. (PR #491)

3. Paying kTown shop QR codes

A kTown QR is an LNURL on our own domain (/.well-known/lnurlp/k-<id>). The wallet saw its own domain and read k-<id> as a wallet name: "No Ye₿ente wallet has that handle."

Now k- means a shop, and the wallet asks kTown for the shop's invoice directly. Going over HTTP to ourselves would have failed anyway: kTown fronts the payout partner, so the invoice commits to the partner's description, not kTown's. New wallets can't take a k- name, so none can pose as a shop. (PR #493)

4. Send and Receive, simpler

  • Send opens on the scanner: continuous focus, tap to focus, torch and zoom where the phone has them, and every other frame a sharp close-up of the middle for small or dense codes. (PR #501)
  • Clipboard offer: copy an invoice or Lightning address and the app offers to paste it. It's read on the phone only, used only if you tap Paste.
  • Approve last: no PIN box on the amount screen. Send opens your fingerprint, or a final PIN pop-up. (PR #503)
  • Receive is one big QR with your address under it, one tap to copy, and an invoice that fills the screen until it's paid. (PR #505)
  • No empty wallet: while the node reconnects, the buttons stay on screen, greyed out. (PR #489)

How it ships

Every change gets an issue, a pull request, tests that fail on the old code first, CI, and a review before merge. The suite is at 779 tests passing. It's all public: github.com/altradits/altradits.

I'm working toward full-time Bitcoin open-source work, learning to review Bitcoin's code alongside building this.

Not sponsored. No paid posts. Try the wallet: altradits.com/yebente

articles.title: The job scanner that marked postings "done" without reading them
articles.description: career-ops is an open-source job-search tool with over 80,000 stars on GitHub. One part of it,...
articles.body_html:
career-ops is an open-source job-search tool with over 80,000 stars on GitHub. One part of it, openrouter-runner, takes the job postings in your pipeline, opens each page in a headless browser, sends the job text to a free model on OpenRouter, and writes a score into your tracker.

On 23 October I ran it on 15 live Workday postings (career-ops v1.37.0). All 15 rows were marked done. All 15 got a report.

Then I counted what the model had actually received.

What the model saw

Between 0 and 397 characters of job text per posting. Six of the 15 got nothing at all. The rest got the page frame, for example:

Skip to main content Loading Follow Us © 2026 Workday, Inc. All rights reserved.

That is 80 characters. No title, no requirements, no description.

The cause was one line. After opening the page, the runner waited a fixed 2 seconds, then read the body. Workday builds the job description with JavaScript after the page loads. When I reran the same postings the next day, the description appeared 5.0 to 9.2 seconds after navigation started, on 13 of the 15. Two seconds was never going to be enough.

Why "done" was the real bug

A slow page is normal. The bug was what happened next: the pipeline treated "the model replied" as "the posting was evaluated".

To show it without any real model, I pointed the runner at three local pages with no job text, and replaced the model with a stub that always answers Score: 4.2/5. All three went out with 0 characters of job text. All three were marked done. The tracker said 4.2/5 | Evaluated.

Nothing in the tracker separates a real score from a score about nothing. Someone reading it would apply, or skip, based on a number that came from an empty page.

A second bug in the same runner

The runner reuses the prompt that career-ops gives to agents that have tools. That prompt tells the model to search the web, run other scripts, check the CV. The runner sends no tools.

So the free models did what the prompt asked. On Workday pages with no description, 19 of 19 replies were tool calls, or said they were about to make one. On real descriptions (7.8K to 16K characters), 4 replies came back: 3 tool calls and 1 empty. Across all 23 replies, the score parser found 0 scores.

How it got fixed

I filed both bugs as issue #5809 on 24 October, with the numbers above and the stub script. Fixing it took four pull requests. Three are mine:

PR What changed Merged
#5814 (by bercedev) A posting that wasn't read is not saved or marked done 25 Oct
#5817 The runner tells the model it has no tools, and strips the steps it can't run 26 Oct
#6017 Model timeout raised from 15 s to 120 s 27 Oct
#6169 Wait for the job description, not for a fixed 2 s 6 Nov

6017 came out of the same work. The 15-second timeout was set in June, when the two prompt files the runner sends added up to about 31K characters. By October they were about 113K. On the free model rotation, a timeout also put the model on a blacklist that survives restarts.

After #5814, the false "done" was gone. But it showed the next problem: with the 2-second wait still there, a Workday posting could never be read, so its row stayed pending forever. I measured 20 live Workday postings, 4 each from NVIDIA, Salesforce, Adobe, Intel and Mastercard:

  • With the fixed 2 s wait: 0 of 20 readable. All refused as too short, in 3 to 4 seconds.
  • With a wait for the job text: 20 of 20 readable, 3,680 to 9,072 characters, in 3.3 to 6.9 seconds.

6169 first tries career-ops' own job-board API reader (Workday, Greenhouse, Lever and others), and only falls back to the browser if that returns nothing. In the browser it waits until the main content holds more than 1,500 visible characters, or until the page clearly says the posting is closed, with a 15-second cap. A 4xx or 5xx page skips the wait.

What review added

The maintainer asked for changes, and the automated reviewer (CodeRabbit) raised findings over several rounds. Not all of it was noise. One finding was real, and it came from my own change: a page with an "Apply now" button and a description still saying "Loading..." could end the wait early. I wrote a test for exactly that page, watched it fail, then fixed it.

6169 was merged on 6 November and shipped in career-ops v1.40.0 on 10 November. On the issue, the maintainer wrote: "Thanks for fixing it yourself."

What I check now, in any pipeline that sends fetched content to a model

  1. Count what the model received. Characters, not "page loaded". It is one log line.
  2. Don't mark work done because a reply came back. Mark it done when the input passed a check.
  3. Don't let the prompt promise tools the code doesn't send. The model will try to use them.
  4. Wait for content, not for a clock. A fixed sleep is a guess about someone else's server.

The tests passed the whole time, and the tracker looked full. That is what made it hard to see.

Links

  • Issue: https://github.com/career-ops-hq/career-ops/issues/5809
  • PRs: #5814, #5817, #6017, #6169
  • Release notes: https://github.com/career-ops-hq/career-ops/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

AI disclosure: I found and fixed these bugs with the help of AI coding tools (Claude Code), and drafted this post with Claude. Every number comes from the linked issue and pull requests, and I checked the text before publishing.

articles.title: Inside a 2.2 KB Signals Runtime: One Graph, One Stack, No Recursion
articles.description: How Reflex Quant derives a small reactive machine from explicit semantics, reusing graph relations for tracking, validation, failure recovery, and traversal.
articles.body_html:
A reactive runtime begins with a simple idea: record dependencies when values are read, then notify consumers when those values change. The difficulty begins when dependencies change order, computations fail halfway through execution, or writes invalidate computations that are still running. Each case invites another flag, index, queue, or special rule. Eventually, much of the runtime exists to coordinate its own bookkeeping.

Reflex Quant began with a different question: What is the smallest machine we can derive from a fixed reactive contract, without inheriting the architecture of an existing implementation?

The result is a JavaScript signals runtime of approximately 2.2 KB gzip. It supports exact dynamic dependencies, glitch-free propagation, computed values that retain state between executions, defined failure recovery, and graph traversal without recursion. Its size is interesting, but the more important result is how many apparently separate mechanisms can share the same representation.

One relation, several responsibilities

Quant separates its implementation into a kernel, a host, and a public API. The kernel owns dependencies and change propagation. The host delivers effects, manages cleanup, and implements batching. The public API exposes these operations without adding another layer of graph objects.

Inside the kernel, the graph has just two object types: Node and Edge.

Every dependency is represented by an edge that belongs to two linked lists simultaneously. Its consumer keeps the edge in dependency-read order, while its source keeps the same object in subscriber-delivery order.

X.deps:   [A → X] ↔ [B → X] ↔ [C → X]
                       │
                       │ same Edge
                       │
B.subs:   [B → W] ↔ [B → X] ↔ [B → Y]

The consumer's list supports tracking and validation. The source's list supports invalidation. There is no second representation to synchronize because both lists contain the same relation.

Each edge also records the source version its consumer observed and the generation in which the relation was confirmed. These fields allow the graph to remember not only who depends on whom, but also what was observed and whether that observation was successfully committed.

This matters when dependencies change dynamically.

A computation that reads A, B, C on one execution might read B, C, A on the next. The dependency set has not changed, so destroying and recreating its edges would be unnecessary. Quant instead retains the relations and changes their order.

On a stable execution, a cursor walks the existing dependency list. Each matching read advances the cursor without allocation or lookup. When the order differs, Quant searches for the existing relation using progressively more expensive exact methods: immediate structural checks, bounded scans, and finally temporary indexing or marking.

The scan limit is a cost limit, not a correctness shortcut. Failing to find an edge within eight steps never proves that the edge does not exist. When necessary, the runtime pays for one linear preparation pass rather than repeatedly searching the same graph.

In the reorder.rotate-256 structural test, Quant creates and removes no relations per pass. The tested alien-signals 3.2.1 implementation relinks 255 per pass. These are counted graph operations, not benchmark timings, and they illustrate a difference in representation rather than an automatic victory in execution speed.

The deeper principle is that an existing relation should not become a new object merely because the computation encountered it in a different order.

Change is evidence, not merely a new value

Quant uses push-pull propagation. Writes propagate invalidation, while reads validate upstream values and execute computations only when necessary.

The distinction matters in a diamond-shaped graph, where two computations depend on one source and a third depends on both. Eagerly recomputing the third after only one branch has updated could expose inconsistent intermediate state.

Quant distinguishes a known need to execute, represented by DIRTY, from possible upstream changes, represented by STALE. Validation resolves that uncertainty before execution. If a computed produces an Object.is-equal result, its version does not change, and the update stops propagating.

Versions also preserve information that value comparisons alone would lose. If a signal changes from A to B and back to A, its value has returned to the starting point, but two committed changes occurred. The consumer's edge still records the earlier version, so the outstanding observation cannot silently disappear.

The same mechanism handles a less obvious case: a computation reads a source, changes it, and reads it again during the same execution.

const a = signal(1);

const c = computed(() => {
  const first = get(a);
  if (first === 1) set(a, 2);
  return first + get(a);
});

get(c); // 3
get(c); // 4
get(c); // 4

The first execution combines the initial observation of 1 with the later value 2. Its result is 3, but that execution cannot be considered settled. The source changed after it was first observed, so another execution is owed.

Quant preserves the version of the first observation for that execution. Reading the source again does not erase the evidence of the intervening change.

This is a semantic obligation, not an optional scheduling preference. The runtime must remember that an execution can finish successfully while still owing another execution.

Failure must not rewrite history

Exceptions create a related problem. Suppose a computed successfully reads A, B, C, then fails during another execution after reading A, D.

Discarding the old dependencies would be incorrect because B or C might change and allow the computation to recover. Ignoring D would also be incorrect because it may be the source responsible for the failure.

Quant retains the last successful dependencies while allowing observations from a failed attempt to remain tentative.

Run 1   A B C   success   A B C committed
Run 2   A D     throws    A B C + D tentative
Run 3   A E     throws    A B C + E tentative

An edge created during execution receives the next generation number. A successful execution advances the node's generation, committing the newly confirmed relations together. A failed execution does not advance it.

The runtime therefore distinguishes committed history from temporary observations without maintaining a separate rollback log. Repeated failures also do not accumulate an unlimited collection of tentative edges.

Effects impose a further constraint. Their cleanup functions may perform irreversible user operations, so Quant validates an effect's entire committed dependency set before running its previous cleanup. A failed validation must not destroy a still-valid lifecycle.

The graph and its version history provide the evidence, while the host controls the lifecycle consequences.

One stack for three different problems

Three operations appear to require separate execution machinery.

Invalidation must traverse downstream subscribers. Validation must descend into upstream dependencies and return. Nested tracking must preserve temporary source slots overwritten by an inner computation.

Quant implements all three using one explicit stack of existing edges.

During propagation, an edge identifies the next branch to visit. During validation, it identifies the return path. During nested tracking, it preserves a displaced indexing slot.

The last case reveals why storing an edge is sufficient. Every edge already contains a reference to its source through edge.from. Saving both the displaced edge and its source would duplicate information that can be recovered directly.

Changing the tracking stack to store only edges reduced peak stack entries from 1,542 to 771 in the project's nested-index test.

More importantly, the same array now serves push, pull, and tracking. None requires recursive graph traversal, so dependency depth is limited by available memory rather than the JavaScript call stack.

This is the central architectural observation of Quant: several operations that look unrelated become simpler when their continuations are represented by the same graph object.

What the measurements show

The design has measurable trade-offs. In the project's 18-scenario CI benchmark, Quant 1.1.2 achieved the following geometric-mean time ratios on November 10, 2026:

Comparison Quant time ratio
Against alien-signals 3.2.1 0.45×
Against Reflex 0.99×
Against the faster rival in each scenario 1.03×

Lower values indicate faster execution. Quant benefits from shared dynamic graphs, branch changes, and avoiding unnecessary relation reconstruction. It does not dominate every workload. Reflex remains approximately 20–21% faster in the measured reorder scenarios, while alien-signals is faster on the clean-read microbenchmark.

A separate, broader experiment offers another perspective. The JS Reactivity Benchmark compares 30 JavaScript reactivity implementations across different workload families. Its published November 10, 2026 report covers 51 scenarios, of which 33 shared core scenarios contribute to the performance leaderboard. Three additional core scenarios were excluded from every participant's score because their evidence was incomplete.

The leading twelve entries were:

Rank Runtime Relative score
1 Reflex Quant 1.07×
2 alien-signals 1.20×
3 Reflex 1.24×
4 Reactively 1.65×
5 Preact Signals 1.67×
6 Vue Reactivity 3.6 RC 1.69×
7 Anod 1.89×
8 ReScript Signals 1.93×
9 Lite Signal 1.95×
10 Maverick Signals 2.00×
11 Vue Reactivity 3.5 2.27×
12 Angular Signals 2.43×

The score is a family-balanced geometric mean of execution time relative to the fastest implementation in each shared scenario. Each workload family receives equal weight, and lower is better. The published figures are medians across three machine sets, with comparisons formed within each machine rather than between unrelated CPUs.

Quant recorded 15 decisive scenario wins and the lowest overall core score, approximately 13% ahead of alien-signals by the report's relative-score comparison. Its score ranged from 1.03× to 1.07× across the three machine sets.

The leaderboard is deliberately narrower than the complete test suite. Thirteen large-graph stress scenarios are reported separately; Quant completed all thirteen. Two lifecycle capability scenarios are also separate, and Quant does not provide the ownership capabilities they require. Unsupported operations are not counted as fast executions, nor are they silently added to the core score.

These distinctions matter. A benchmark can compare implementations only over a defined common contract. The result does not establish that a complete Vue, Angular, or Solid application will execute in the same proportions, nor does it measure rendering performance. It describes the tested reactive adapters under specific graph workloads and measurement rules.

The two benchmark suites use different workloads and scoring methods, so their aggregate ratios should not be combined. What they independently support is a narrower architectural conclusion: Quant's compact representation remains competitive across both targeted mechanisms and a broader collection of reactive graph workloads.

What the experiment establishes

Correctness was examined separately from performance. Quant was checked against an executable specification on 27,061 bounded programs, 18,660 recovery programs, and 100,000 generated programs, with graph integrity checked after each operation.

The project also tested 34 mechanism ablations. Every removal violated at least one semantic, structural, representation, or ordering test.

This does not prove that Quant is the smallest possible reactive runtime. An ablation establishes that a mechanism is necessary to this implementation under its current representation and obligations, unless something else replaces its role. Another architecture may satisfy the same contract differently.

Nor is Quant a complete framework. Effect scopes, rendering, ownership trees, asynchronous resources, and transactional updates remain outside its kernel. Those responsibilities are not inherently unimportant; they belong to different layers of the system.

The experiment suggests a broader lesson about software architecture. We often optimize by making individual operations faster, while leaving their separate representations unquestioned. Yet many costs arise because the same fact is stored repeatedly, then synchronized across subsystems.

Quant takes the opposite approach. Dependency order, observed versions, committed history, temporary indexing, and traversal continuations are derived from a small graph whose objects carry several responsibilities.

The price is that correctness depends on strong invariants shared across those responsibilities. Fewer mechanisms do not eliminate complexity. They concentrate it where it can be specified, tested, and examined.

A runtime becomes simpler not necessarily by solving fewer problems, but by storing each truth in one place.

The interactive anatomy of Reflex Quant illustrates these mechanisms with executable examples, dependency diagrams, and a shared-stack visualization.

The complete source code, semantic contract, research report, 18-scenario CI benchmarks, and broader JS Reactivity Benchmark are public.

Reflex Quant is MIT-licensed and published on npm. It remains a research-driven implementation rather than a library with an established history of production deployment.
